board_events.text: A sideways force would make the fluid slide and flow.
No sideways force survives in a fluid at rest.
Force is a vector; pressure is a scalar.
Same pressure whichever way the surface faces.

segments.text: <curious> What exactly is pressure? Picture standing in a packed train, squeezed inward from every side at once.
A tiny water droplet sitting deep inside a tank feels exactly that: the surrounding fluid presses on it from all directions.
Take any small flat surface submerged in the fluid. The force the fluid pushes with is always perpendicular, never sideways.
If there were a sideways component, the fluid would simply slide and flow, so it would no longer be at rest.
For a static fluid, only the normal force survives on any surface you place inside it.
So pressure equals the perpendicular force divided by area, measured in pascals, newtons per square metre.
<excited> Here is the exam favourite: force is a vector, but pressure has no direction of its own, so it is a scalar.
That is why a diver eardrum feels the same pressure facing up, down, or sideways at a given depth.
<curious> Pressure असल में है क्या? सोचो एक खचाखच भरी train में तुम हर side से inward squeeze feel करते हो।
एक tiny water droplet जो tank में deep बैठी है, उसे बिल्कुल वैसा ही feel होता है, चारों तरफ से fluid उस पर press करता है।
कोई भी small flat surface fluid में डुबो दो। Fluid जिस force से push करता है वो हमेशा perpendicular होता है, कभी sideways नहीं।
अगर कोई sideways component होता, तो fluid slide करके flow करने लगता, यानी वो at rest रहता ही नहीं।
Static fluid में, अंदर रखी किसी भी surface पर सिर्फ normal force ही survive करती है।
तो pressure equals perpendicular force divided by area, pascals में measure होता है, यानी newtons per square metre।
<excited> ये रहा exam का favourite point: force एक vector है, पर pressure की अपनी कोई direction नहीं होती, इसलिए वो एक scalar है।
इसीलिए एक diver का eardrum किसी given depth पर up, down या sideways, हर तरफ same pressure feel करता है।

board_events.text: Pressure rises steadily as you descend.
Pressure grows linearly with depth h.
Surface: atmosphere alone. Deeper: atmosphere plus column.
Depends on depth and density, not on total volume.

segments.text: <curious> Why does pressure grow as you go deeper? Think of the overhead tank on a rooftop.
The water at the bottom has to support the weight of all the water sitting above it.
So the deeper you go, the taller the column of fluid pressing down, and the greater the pressure.
This is the single most important idea of the subtopic: pressure increases as you descend.
Absolute pressure equals atmospheric pressure P naught plus rho g h, where h is the depth.
And it grows linearly, in a straight line, with the depth h.
At the free surface you feel only the atmosphere. A depth h below, you feel the atmosphere plus the weight of the column above.
<excited> Crucially, it depends on depth and density, never on the total volume of liquid.
<curious> गहराई में जाते ही pressure क्यों बढ़ता है? Rooftop के overhead tank को सोचो।
नीचे के water को उसके ऊपर बैठे सारे water का weight support करना पड़ता है।
तो जितना deep जाओगे, उतना taller fluid का column ऊपर से press करेगा, और pressure उतना ज़्यादा।
यही इस subtopic की सबसे important idea है: नीचे जाते ही pressure बढ़ता जाता है।
Absolute pressure equals atmospheric pressure P naught plus rho g h, जहाँ h है depth।
और ये linearly बढ़ता है, यानी सीधी line में, depth h के साथ।
Free surface पर सिर्फ atmosphere feel होता है। Depth h नीचे, atmosphere plus ऊपर वाले column का weight।
<excited> सबसे ज़रूरी: ये depth और density पर depend करता है, कभी total volume पर नहीं।

Yet they hold very different amounts of water.

Shape and volume never enter.

segments.text: <curious> Now a beautifully counter-intuitive result, the hydrostatic paradox.
Take three vessels of wildly different shapes: narrow and tall, wide and squat, and funnel-shaped.
Fill all three with water to exactly the same height.
The pressure at the base comes out identical in all three vessels.
Students find this shocking, since the vessels clearly hold completely different amounts of water.
But base pressure depends only on the depth below the surface and the density of the fluid.
The gauge pressure at the base is simply rho g h, and nothing more.
The container shape and the total volume never enter the formula. Same height means same pressure.
<curious> अब एक बड़ा ही counter-intuitive result, hydrostatic paradox।
तीन vessels लो एकदम अलग shapes की: narrow और tall, wide और squat, और funnel जैसी।
तीनों को water से बिल्कुल same height तक भर दो।
Base पर pressure तीनों vessels में identical निकलता है।
Students को ये shocking लगता है, क्योंकि तीनों में water की quantity साफ़ अलग है।
पर base pressure सिर्फ surface से नीचे की depth और fluid की density पर depend करता है।
Base पर gauge pressure simply rho g h है, बस इतना ही।
Container का shape और total volume formula में कभी नहीं आते। Same height यानी same pressure।

board_events.text: Transmitted undiminished, everywhere.
The hydraulic lift: small push, big lift.
Bigger output area means a bigger lifting force.
Force is multiplied, energy is conserved.

segments.text: <curious> This second great idea belongs to Blaise Pascal.
Push a piston into a sealed bottle of water, and the extra pressure does not stay near the piston.
It spreads undiminished to every single point in the fluid and onto every wall of the container.
Squeeze one end of a toothpaste tube and the paste shoots out the far end. That is Pascal law in everyday action.
The hydraulic lift is the payoff. Push a small input piston, and the pressure reaches a large output piston.
The output force equals the input force times the area ratio, A two over A one.
Because the output area is bigger, a small push can lift a heavy car.
But energy is never created. The small piston travels farther, so the work done stays equal.
<curious> ये दूसरी बड़ी idea Blaise Pascal की है।
एक sealed bottle में piston दबाओ, तो वो extra pressure piston के पास नहीं रुकता।
वो undiminished होकर fluid के हर एक point पर और container की हर wall पर फैल जाता है।
Toothpaste tube का एक सिरा दबाओ, paste दूसरे सिरे से निकलता है। यही रोज़मर्रा में Pascal law है।
Hydraulic lift इसका payoff है। छोटे input piston को दबाओ, pressure बड़े output piston तक पहुँचता है।
Output force equals input force times area ratio, A two over A one।
Output area बड़ा है, इसलिए एक छोटा push एक भारी car उठा सकता है।
पर energy कभी create नहीं होती। छोटा piston ज़्यादा distance चलता है, तो किया गया work equal रहता है।

board_events.text: Down: P1 A on top. Up: P2 A on bottom. Down: weight.

board_events.latex: P_2 A = P_1 A + \rho A (h_2 - h_1)\,g

board_events.text: Cancel the common area A from every term.
Put the top at the surface: P = P0 + rho g h.
Depends on depth alone, the root of the paradox.

segments.text: <curious> Let us actually derive the depth law from a simple force balance.
Isolate an imaginary thin cylindrical column of fluid of cross-section area A. Since the fluid is at rest, this column is in equilibrium.
Three vertical forces act on it. Look carefully at the free-body diagram.
The fluid above pushes down with P one times A. The fluid below pushes up with P two times A. And the column own weight pulls down.
The upward push must support both the downward push and the weight, so P two A equals P one A plus rho A times the height difference times g.
Now cancel the common area A from every term.
That leaves P two minus P one equals rho g times the height difference.
Choose the top face at the free surface, where the pressure is P naught, and let the bottom sit at depth h. You reach P equals P naught plus rho g h.
The result depends only on depth, not on the cross-section. That is exactly the origin of the hydrostatic paradox.
<curious> चलो depth law को एक simple force balance से actually derive करते हैं।
एक imaginary thin cylindrical column लो, cross-section area A। Fluid at rest है, तो ये column equilibrium में है।
इस पर तीन vertical forces act करती हैं। Free-body diagram को ध्यान से देखो।
ऊपर का fluid P one times A से नीचे push करता है। नीचे का fluid P two times A से ऊपर। और column का अपना weight नीचे खींचता है।
Upward push को downward push और weight दोनों support करने हैं, तो P two A equals P one A plus rho A times height difference times g।
अब हर term से common area A cancel कर दो।
बचता है P two minus P one equals rho g times height difference।
Top face को free surface पर रखो, जहाँ pressure P naught है, और bottom को depth h पर। मिलता है P equals P naught plus rho g h।
Result सिर्फ depth पर depend करता है, cross-section पर नहीं। यही hydrostatic paradox की असली जड़ है।

board_events.text: The pressure toolkit
Absolute is never negative; gauge can be.

segments.text: <curious> Let us gather the whole toolkit for this subtopic in one place.
First, pressure itself: the perpendicular force divided by area, in pascals.
The depth law: absolute pressure equals P naught plus rho g h.
Gauge pressure is the pressure above atmospheric, equal to rho g h. It is what a tyre gauge reads.
Absolute pressure is always positive; but gauge pressure can go negative, as when you suck on a straw.
For the hydraulic lift, the pressure is shared, so F one over A one equals F two over A two.
And the same volume of fluid moves at both pistons, so A one h one equals A two h two.
Keep one conversion handy: one atmosphere is about one point zero one three times ten to the fifth pascals, or seven hundred sixty millimetres of mercury.
<curious> इस subtopic का पूरा toolkit एक जगह इकट्ठा कर लेते हैं।
पहले pressure खुद: perpendicular force divided by area, pascals में।
Depth law: absolute pressure equals P naught plus rho g h।
Gauge pressure यानी atmospheric से ऊपर का pressure, equal to rho g h। यही tyre gauge दिखाता है।
Absolute pressure हमेशा positive; पर gauge pressure negative भी हो सकता है, जैसे straw से sip करते वक़्त।
Hydraulic lift के लिए pressure share होता है, तो F one over A one equals F two over A two।
और same volume दोनों pistons पर move होता है, तो A one h one equals A two h two।
एक conversion याद रखो: one atmosphere लगभग one point zero one three times ten to the fifth pascals, या seven hundred sixty millimetres of mercury।

segments.text: <curious> A clean C B S E board problem, a hostel overhead tank.
Water fills it to two point five metres. The circular base has area zero point eight square metres, and atmospheric pressure is one times ten to the fifth pascals.
We want the gauge pressure at the base, the absolute pressure there, and the total downward force on the base.
Part a, the gauge pressure is simply rho g h.
That is one thousand times ten times two point five, giving two point five times ten to the fourth pascals.
Part b, the absolute pressure adds the atmosphere back in.
One times ten to the fifth plus zero point two five times ten to the fifth gives one point two five times ten to the fifth pascals.
<whisper> Now the subtle point: the force on the base uses the absolute pressure, because the atmosphere presses down too, transmitted through the water.
Force equals pressure times area: one point two five times ten to the fifth, times zero point eight, gives one times ten to the fifth newtons.
<curious> एक साफ़-सुथरा C B S E board problem, एक hostel का overhead tank।
Water उसमें two point five metres तक भरा है। Circular base का area zero point eight square metres, और atmospheric pressure one times ten to the fifth pascals।
हमें चाहिए base पर gauge pressure, वहाँ absolute pressure, और base पर total downward force।
Part a, gauge pressure simply rho g h है।
यानी one thousand times ten times two point five, जो देता है two point five times ten to the fourth pascals।
Part b, absolute pressure में atmosphere वापस add करते हैं।
One times ten to the fifth plus zero point two five times ten to the fifth gives one point two five times ten to the fifth pascals।
<whisper> अब बारीक point: base पर force absolute pressure use करता है, क्योंकि atmosphere भी water के through नीचे press करता है।
Force equals pressure times area: one point two five times ten to the fifth, times zero point eight, gives one times ten to the fifth newtons।

segments.text: <curious> A quick N E E T speed trap, a scuba diver in seawater.
At what depth does the gauge pressure equal two atmospheres? The seawater density is one thousand thirty.
First trap: the question asks for gauge pressure, so use rho g h directly, with no atmospheric term.
Second trap: use the seawater density, one thousand thirty, not fresh water one thousand.
Rearranging the gauge relation, depth equals gauge pressure divided by rho g.
That is two times ten to the fifth, over one thousand thirty times ten, which is about nineteen point four metres.
<whisper> A shortcut worth memorising: in water rho g is close to ten to the fourth, so each atmosphere of gauge pressure costs about ten metres of depth.
Two atmospheres means roughly twenty metres, nudged slightly down because seawater is denser than fresh water.

segments.text: <curious> Now a J E E Main favourite, the hydraulic car lift.
The input piston has radius two centimetres, the output radius twenty centimetres, and a car of mass twelve hundred kilograms rests on the output.
Part a: the input force needed to just support the car. Part b: how far the input piston must move to raise the car by five centimetres.
The output force simply equals the car weight, m g.
That is twelve hundred times ten, or one point two times ten to the fourth newtons.
Areas scale as radius squared, so the area ratio is twenty over two, all squared, which is one hundred.
By Pascal law, the input force is the output force divided by one hundred, giving one hundred twenty newtons.
For part b, the same fluid volume moves at both pistons, so the small piston travels a hundred times farther.
Five centimetres times one hundred is five hundred centimetres, that is five metres.
<whisper> Energy check: input work is one hundred twenty times five, six hundred joules, equal to the output work. The lift multiplies force, never energy.

Part a: car को just support करने के लिए ज़रूरी input force। Part b: car को five centimetres उठाने के लिए input piston कितना move करे।

Pascal law से, input force output force divided by one hundred है, जो one hundred twenty newtons देता है।

Five centimetres times one hundred is five hundred centimetres, यानी five metres।
<whisper> Energy check: input work one hundred twenty times five, यानी six hundred joules, output work के बराबर। Lift force multiply करता है, energy कभी नहीं।

board_events.text: Drop x on the left, rise x on the right: difference 2x.
Balance pressures at the lower mercury surface.
Mercury rises 0.5 cm right, falls 0.5 cm left.

segments.text: <curious> A J E E Advanced classic, the multi-liquid U-tube, and it hides a trap.
Both arms are open. Mercury sits in the tube, and a water column of height thirteen point six centimetres is poured into the left arm, floating on the mercury.
Here is the key insight. When mercury is pushed down by x in the left arm, that same mercury reappears in the right arm, rising by x.
So the difference in mercury levels between the two arms is two x, not x. Miss this and your answer comes out exactly half wrong.
Balance the pressure at the level of the lower mercury surface. Both sides must be equal at the same horizontal level.
The left side gives P naught plus rho water g H. The right side gives P naught plus rho mercury g times two x.
The P naught terms cancel, so two x equals H times the density ratio, thirteen point six times one thousand over thirteen thousand six hundred, which is one point zero centimetre.
Therefore x is zero point five centimetre.
The mercury rises half a centimetre on the right and falls half a centimetre on the left. The clean cancellation confirms you handled the two x correctly.
<curious> एक J E E Advanced classic, multi-liquid U-tube, और इसमें एक trap छिपा है।
दोनों arms open हैं। Mercury tube में है, और thirteen point six centimetres का एक water column left arm में डाला जाता है, mercury पर floating।
यहाँ key insight है। जब mercury left arm में x नीचे धकेला जाता है, वही mercury right arm में x ऊपर आ जाता है।
तो दोनों arms के बीच mercury level का difference two x है, x नहीं। ये चूके तो answer बिल्कुल आधा गलत आएगा।
Lower mercury surface के level पर pressure balance करो। दोनों sides same horizontal level पर equal होनी चाहिए।
Left side देता है P naught plus rho water g H। Right side देता है P naught plus rho mercury g times two x।
P naught terms cancel हो जाते हैं, तो two x equals H times density ratio, thirteen point six times one thousand over thirteen thousand six hundred, यानी one point zero centimetre।
इसलिए x is zero point five centimetre।
Mercury right में आधा centimetre ऊपर और left में आधा centimetre नीचे जाता है। ये clean cancellation confirm करता है कि two x सही handle हुआ।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: pressure and Pascal

board_events.text: Pitfalls and pro-tips
Pressure is a scalar; only its force is a vector.
Tyre, blood, and submarine pressures are gauge.
More liquid does not mean more pressure.
U-tube: a drop of x gives a 2x level difference.
Pro-tip: in water, about 1 atm of gauge per 10 m.
Sanity-check depth answers in your head with this.

segments.text: <curious> Let us lock in the classic traps for this subtopic.
First, never treat pressure as a vector. Pressure is a scalar; only the force it produces is a vector, and that force always acts perpendicular to the surface.
Second, gauge versus absolute. Tyre pressure, blood pressure, and submarine window pressure are almost always gauge values, measured above the atmosphere.
Third, do not fall for the hydrostatic paradox. More liquid does not mean more pressure. The base pressure depends only on rho, g, and the height h.
Fourth, the U-tube factor of two. When fluid drops by x on one side, it rises by x on the other, so the level difference is two x. This single slip makes Advanced answers come out half wrong.
<whisper> And the pro-tip worth its weight in marks: in water, rho g is about ten to the fourth, so roughly one atmosphere of gauge pressure per ten metres of depth.
Use that to sanity-check any depth answer in your head before grinding the arithmetic, and to instantly flag a wrong order of magnitude.
<curious> इस subtopic के classic traps पक्के कर लेते हैं।
पहला, pressure को कभी vector मत मानो। Pressure एक scalar है; सिर्फ उसकी बनाई force vector है, और वो force हमेशा surface के perpendicular act करती है।
दूसरा, gauge versus absolute। Tyre pressure, blood pressure, और submarine window pressure लगभग हमेशा gauge values होती हैं, atmosphere से ऊपर measure।
तीसरा, hydrostatic paradox में मत फँसो। ज़्यादा liquid का मतलब ज़्यादा pressure नहीं। Base pressure सिर्फ rho, g और height h पर depend करता है।
चौथा, U-tube का factor of two। जब fluid एक side x गिरता है, दूसरी side x उठता है, तो level difference two x है। यही एक चूक Advanced answers आधे गलत कर देती है।
<whisper> और marks दिलाने वाला pro-tip: water में rho g करीब ten to the fourth है, तो लगभग one atmosphere gauge pressure per ten metres depth।
इसका use करके किसी भी depth answer को दिमाग़ में sanity-check करो, arithmetic से पहले, और गलत order of magnitude तुरंत पकड़ो।

Push it deeper and it shoves back harder.

board_events.text: Pressure on the bottom face exceeds that on the top.
Bottom is deeper, so the upward push wins.
The leftover net upward force is buoyancy.
No pressure gradient, no buoyancy.

segments.text: <curious> Ever tried to push a beach ball down to the bottom of a pool? It fights back, hard.
The deeper you push it, the more stubbornly it shoves upward, and the moment you let go it rockets to the surface.
That upward shove is buoyancy, and it is not a new mysterious force. It is just the fluid pressure you already met.
Recall that pressure rises with depth. So on any submerged object, the pressure on the bottom face is larger than on the top face.
That is the depth law again: P equals P naught plus rho g h, bigger wherever h is bigger.
Since the bottom sits deeper, the upward push from below beats the downward push from above.
The leftover, the net upward force, is exactly the buoyant force.
<excited> So buoyancy exists only because pressure varies with depth. No pressure gradient means no buoyancy at all.
<curious> कभी beach ball को pool की तली तक धकेलने की कोशिश की? वो ज़ोर से वापस लड़ता है।
जितना deep धकेलोगे, उतना ज़िद्दी होकर वो ऊपर धकेलता है, और छोड़ते ही surface पर rocket की तरह आता है।
वो upward shove ही buoyancy है, और ये कोई नई mysterious force नहीं। ये तो वही fluid pressure है जो तुम पहले मिल चुके हो।
याद करो pressure depth के साथ बढ़ता है। तो किसी भी submerged object पर, bottom face का pressure top face से बड़ा होता है।
यही depth law फिर से: P equals P naught plus rho g h, जहाँ h बड़ा वहाँ pressure बड़ा।
Bottom deeper है, इसलिए नीचे से upward push ऊपर से downward push को हरा देता है।
जो बचता है, वो net upward force, बिल्कुल वही buoyant force है।
<excited> तो buoyancy सिर्फ इसलिए है क्योंकि pressure depth के साथ बदलता है। No pressure gradient, तो कोई buoyancy नहीं।

Fluid does not know what is inside the boundary.

segments.text: <curious> Here is the elegant argument behind Archimedes principle.
Imagine scooping out the object and replacing it with an identical blob of the same fluid, a water-shaped lump of water.
That blob just floats there in equilibrium. It neither sinks nor rises, because it is simply part of the fluid.
What holds it up? The surrounding fluid pushes on its boundary with exactly enough upward force to balance the blob own weight.
But the surrounding fluid does not know what is inside that boundary. It pushes the same way for water or for an iron block.
So the upward force on any object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. Buoyancy equals rho fluid times submerged volume times g.
This is Archimedes principle, and it acts vertically upward through the centre of the displaced fluid.
<excited> Notice: it uses the fluid density and the submerged volume, never the body own density.
<curious> ये रहा Archimedes principle के पीछे का elegant argument।
सोचो object को निकालकर उसकी जगह वही fluid का identical blob रख दो, यानी water के shape का water का lump।
वो blob वहीं equilibrium में रहता है। न डूबता, न उठता, क्योंकि वो तो fluid का ही हिस्सा है।
उसे कौन थामे रखता है? आसपास का fluid उसकी boundary पर ठीक उतना upward force देता है जो blob के weight को balance करे।
पर आसपास का fluid नहीं जानता boundary के अंदर क्या है। वो water हो या iron block, same तरीके से push करता है।
तो किसी भी object पर upward force उतना ही होता है जितना displaced fluid का weight। Buoyancy equals rho fluid times submerged volume times g।
यही Archimedes principle है, और ये displaced fluid के centre से vertically upward act करता है।
<excited> ध्यान दो: ये fluid density और submerged volume use करता है, कभी body की अपनी density नहीं।

board_events.text: Denser than the fluid: weight wins, it sinks.
Equal density: it hovers, fully submerged.
Lighter: buoyancy wins, it rises and floats.
A steel ship floats; a steel nail sinks.
Average density relative to the fluid decides everything.

segments.text: <curious> So what actually decides whether something floats or sinks?
The buoyant force itself uses only the fluid. The body own density enters only to decide the outcome.
Compare the two densities. Three cases follow.
If the body is denser than the fluid, its weight beats the maximum possible buoyancy, and it sinks.
If the densities are exactly equal, it hovers, floating fully submerged, in equilibrium anywhere.
If the body is lighter, buoyancy wins. It rises until just enough pokes out that the reduced submerged volume balances its weight. That is floatation.
This is why a giant steel ship floats while a small steel nail sinks. The nail is solid steel, denser than water; the ship is mostly hollow.
<excited> Same material, opposite fate, decided entirely by the average density relative to the fluid.
<curious> तो असल में क्या decide करता है कि कोई चीज़ floats करेगी या sinks?
Buoyant force खुद सिर्फ fluid use करती है। Body की अपनी density सिर्फ outcome decide करने आती है।
दोनों densities compare करो। तीन cases बनते हैं।

segments.text: <curious> Let us pin down exactly how much of a floating body sits underwater.
At floatation, the body weight equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.
Write that balance: rho body times V times g equals rho fluid times submerged volume times g.

तो relative density zero point six वाला block अपने sixty percent हिस्से के साथ underwater floats करता है।
<excited> इसीलिए एक iceberg का लगभग ninety percent surface के नीचे छिपा रहता है।

segments.text: <curious> What happens to buoyancy inside a lift or a turning car?
The simple rule, buoyancy equals the weight of displaced fluid, needs the fluid in an inertial frame. When it accelerates, replace g with an effective gravity.
Picture a cork tied to the base of a beaker inside an accelerating lift.
The buoyant force becomes rho fluid times submerged volume times g effective.
For a lift accelerating up, g effective is g plus a. For one accelerating down, it is g minus a.
<excited> And in free fall, g effective is zero, so there is no pressure gradient and buoyancy vanishes entirely.
Everything else about floatation carries over untouched. You only swap in the effective gravity.

एक cork सोचो जो accelerating lift के अंदर beaker की base से बँधा है।
Buoyant force बन जाती है rho fluid times submerged volume times g effective।
ऊपर accelerate करती lift में g effective is g plus a। नीचे accelerate करती में g minus a।
<excited> और free fall में g effective zero है, तो कोई pressure gradient नहीं और buoyancy पूरी तरह ग़ायब।
Floatation का बाकी सब वैसे ही रहता है। तुम बस effective gravity swap करते हो।

board_events.text: The buoyancy toolkit
Sink if the body is denser; float if it is lighter.
For a floater, write weight = displaced-fluid weight first.

segments.text: <curious> Let us assemble the buoyancy toolkit in one place.
The buoyant force: rho fluid times submerged volume times g. Fluid density and submerged volume, always.
Apparent weight is the real weight minus buoyancy, which equals V g times the density difference, rho body minus rho fluid.
The submerged fraction of a floater equals the density ratio, rho body over rho fluid.
Relative density is rho body over rho water, and neatly, weight in air divided by the loss of weight in water. No volume needed.
The floatation rule in one line: sink if the body is denser than the fluid, float if it is lighter.
In an accelerating frame, just swap g for g effective in the buoyancy formula.
<whisper> The master move for any floating problem: write weight of the body equals weight of displaced fluid, then substitute.
<curious> Buoyancy का पूरा toolkit एक जगह इकट्ठा कर लेते हैं।
Buoyant force: rho fluid times submerged volume times g। हमेशा fluid density और submerged volume।
Apparent weight यानी real weight minus buoyancy, जो equals V g times density difference, rho body minus rho fluid।
Floater का submerged fraction equals density ratio, rho body over rho fluid।
Relative density है rho body over rho water, और सफ़ाई से, weight in air divided by loss of weight in water। कोई volume नहीं चाहिए।
Floatation rule एक line में: body fluid से denser हो तो sink, lighter हो तो float।
Accelerating frame में, buoyancy formula में g की जगह g effective रख दो।
<whisper> किसी भी floating problem का master move: पहले लिखो weight of body equals weight of displaced fluid, फिर substitute करो।

board_events.text: Pitfalls and pro-tips
Buoyancy uses fluid density and submerged volume, not the body's.
Submerged fraction is rho_b over rho_f, not the inverse.
Floating ice melting in its own water: level unchanged.
But ice with a stone, or in a different liquid, does change it.
Accelerating frame: buoyancy scales with g_eff, not g.
Master line: weight of body = weight of displaced fluid.

segments.text: <curious> Let us lock in the buoyancy traps.
First, and most common: buoyancy uses the fluid density and the submerged volume. The body own density only decides sink versus float, never the size of the upthrust.
Second, the submerged fraction is rho body over rho fluid, not the inverse. A quick check: a floater has this fraction below one. If you get more than one, you flipped it.
Third, the ice-melting trap. Floating ice melting in its own water leaves the level unchanged, because the melt water exactly fills the volume it displaced.
But watch the variations: ice with a stone embedded, or ice floating in a different liquid like mercury or brine, do change the level. Do not apply unchanged blindly.
Fourth, in a lift or a turning car, buoyancy scales with g effective, not g. In free fall, g effective is zero, and a submerged cork no longer rises.
<whisper> The one master line for every floating problem: weight of the body equals weight of the displaced fluid. Write it first, then substitute.
<curious> Buoyancy के traps पक्के कर लेते हैं।
पहला, और सबसे common: buoyancy fluid density और submerged volume use करती है। Body की density सिर्फ sink versus float decide करती है, upthrust का size कभी नहीं।
दूसरा, submerged fraction rho body over rho fluid है, उल्टा नहीं। Quick check: floater का ये fraction one से कम होता है। एक से ज़्यादा आए तो तुमने flip कर दिया।
तीसरा, ice-melting trap। अपने ही पानी में floating ice पिघले तो level unchanged रहता है, क्योंकि melt water ठीक वही volume भरता है जो उसने displace किया था।
पर variations देखो: stone जड़ी ice, या mercury या brine जैसे अलग liquid में floating ice, level बदल देती हैं। Unchanged को आँख मूँदकर मत लगाओ।
चौथा, lift या मुड़ती car में buoyancy g effective के साथ scale करती है, g के साथ नहीं। Free fall में g effective zero, और submerged cork अब नहीं उठता।
<whisper> हर floating problem की एक master line: weight of body equals weight of displaced fluid। पहले लिखो, फिर substitute करो।

sections.title: Effective gravity: one trick for all

board_events.text: Effective gravity: one trick for all
In an accelerating fluid, the surface is no longer flat.

board_events.caption: Gravity plus pseudo-force gives g_eff

<text x="95" y="170" fill="#2f7d5a" font-size="12">g_eff</text>

<text x="250" y="150" fill="#2b6ca3" font-size="12">free surface, perpendicular to g_eff</text>
<text x="200" y="255" text-anchor="middle" fill="#22303c" font-size="12">g_eff = square root of (a squared + g squared)</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Combine real gravity with a pseudo-force into g_eff.
The free surface always sits perpendicular to g_eff.
Measure depth along g_eff and all statics still works.

segments.text: <curious> Everything so far assumed the fluid was perfectly still. What if it moves with its container?
Petrol sloshing in an accelerating tanker, tea tilting as a train pulls away, water climbing a spinning bucket. The surface is no longer flat.
Yet one wonderfully simple trick handles all of it: replace ordinary gravity with an effective gravity.
Ordinary gravity pulls down with g. In the accelerating frame, a pseudo-force pulls the other way with a, per unit mass.
Combine them and the effective gravity has magnitude root of a squared plus g squared, pointing down and backward.
<excited> And the golden rule: a liquid surface at rest in its own frame always sits perpendicular to the effective gravity.
So point your mental down along g effective, measure depth along it, and every fluid-statics result you know still holds.
<curious> अब तक हमने माना fluid बिल्कुल still है। पर अगर वो अपने container के साथ move करे तो?
Accelerating tanker में petrol छलकता, train चलते ही tea झुकती, spinning bucket में पानी दीवार चढ़ता। Surface अब flat नहीं रहती।
फिर भी एक बड़ी simple trick सब संभाल लेती है: ordinary gravity की जगह effective gravity रख दो।
Ordinary gravity g से नीचे खींचती है। Accelerating frame में एक pseudo-force उल्टी ओर a से खींचती है, per unit mass।
इन्हें जोड़ो और effective gravity का magnitude root of a squared plus g squared होता है, down और backward की ओर।
<excited> और golden rule: अपने frame में rest पर liquid surface हमेशा effective gravity के perpendicular बैठती है।
तो अपना mental down g effective के साथ रखो, उसी के साथ depth measure करो, और हर fluid-statics result जस का तस चलता है।

board_events.text: Horizontal acceleration tilts the surface
The water lags and piles at the rear.

board_events.text: Steeper acceleration means a steeper tilt.
At a = g the surface tilts a full 45 degrees.
The liquid rises at the rear, opposite the motion.

segments.text: <curious> Take a tank of water on a cart that suddenly accelerates forward.
The water lags behind. It piles up at the rear and dips at the front, exactly as you lurch backward when a bus jerks forward.
Why this particular angle? Because the surface must sit perpendicular to the effective gravity, which points down and backward.
The tilt angle satisfies tan theta equals a over g.
The faster you accelerate, the steeper the tilt.
If you could accelerate at a equal to g, the surface would tilt a full forty five degrees, since the tangent is one.
Over a tank of length L, the end-to-end height difference is L times tan theta, that is a L over g.
<excited> And mind the direction: the liquid rises at the rear, opposite to the motion, never at the front.
<curious> एक cart पर पानी का tank लो जो अचानक आगे accelerate करती है।
पानी पीछे रह जाता है। वो rear में इकट्ठा होता है और front में dip करता है, ठीक वैसे जैसे bus झटका देती है तो तुम पीछे लुढ़कते हो।
ये खास angle क्यों? क्योंकि surface को effective gravity के perpendicular बैठना है, जो down और backward point करती है।
Tilt angle satisfy करता है tan theta equals a over g।
जितना तेज़ accelerate करोगे, tilt उतना steep।
अगर a equal to g पर accelerate कर सको, surface पूरे forty five degrees झुकेगी, क्योंकि tangent one है।
Length L के tank पर, end to end height difference L times tan theta, यानी a L over g।
<excited> और direction का ध्यान: liquid rear में उठता है, motion के उल्टा, कभी front में नहीं।

board_events.text: Vertical acceleration and free fall
Vertical acceleration strengthens or weakens gravity.

board_events.caption: g + a upward, g - a downward

board_events.text: In free fall, g_eff = 0: no hydrostatic pressure.
Only the surface pressure remains in free fall.

segments.text: <curious> Now push the fluid straight up or straight down instead of sideways.
A vertical acceleration does not tilt the surface; it changes how strong gravity feels.
The effective gravity becomes g plus or minus a.
Plus for upward acceleration, when the fluid feels heavier, and minus for downward.
So the pressure at depth h becomes P naught plus rho times g plus or minus a, times h.
<whisper> The dramatic case is free fall. Here a equals g downward, so g effective is zero.
The fluid becomes effectively weightless and exerts no hydrostatic pressure at all. Only the surface pressure remains.
<curious> अब fluid को sideways की जगह सीधे ऊपर या नीचे धकेलो।
Vertical acceleration surface को झुकाती नहीं; वो बदलती है कि gravity कितनी strong feel होती है।
Effective gravity बन जाती है g plus or minus a।
Upward acceleration के लिए plus, जब fluid heavier feel करे, और downward के लिए minus।
तो depth h पर pressure बन जाता है P naught plus rho times g plus or minus a, times h।
<whisper> Dramatic case है free fall। यहाँ a equals g downward, तो g effective zero।
Fluid effectively weightless हो जाता है और कोई hydrostatic pressure नहीं देता। सिर्फ surface pressure बचता है।

board_events.text: Spin makes a paraboloid
Each parcel needs an inward centripetal force to circle.

board_events.text: Pressure rises outward, so the rim rises.
The free surface curves into a paraboloid.
Faster spin: deeper central dip, higher rim.
Liquid-mirror telescopes use exactly this.

segments.text: <curious> Now spin instead of push. Put water in a cylinder and rotate it steadily about its vertical axis.
Each parcel of water travels in a circle, so it needs a net inward, centripetal force.
The only thing that can supply that inward force is a sideways pressure difference.
So the pressure must increase outward, toward the rim. Higher pressure at the rim means the water level rises there and sinks at the centre.
<excited> The free surface curves into a paraboloid, that elegant bowl shape you see in a stirred cup of tea.
The faster the spin, the deeper the central dip and the higher the rim.
This is exactly why liquid-mirror telescopes spin a dish of mercury: rotation sculpts a perfect parabolic reflector for free.
<curious> अब push की जगह spin करो। एक cylinder में पानी डालो और उसे vertical axis पर steadily घुमाओ।
पानी का हर parcel circle में चलता है, तो उसे एक net inward, centripetal force चाहिए।
वो inward force सिर्फ एक sideways pressure difference ही दे सकता है।
तो pressure बाहर की ओर, rim तक बढ़ना चाहिए। Rim पर ज़्यादा pressure यानी वहाँ level ऊपर और centre पर नीचे।
<excited> Free surface एक paraboloid में मुड़ जाती है, वही elegant bowl shape जो stirred चाय में दिखती है।
जितना तेज़ spin, उतना deeper central dip और उतना higher rim।
इसीलिए liquid-mirror telescopes mercury की dish घुमाते हैं: rotation मुफ़्त में perfect parabolic reflector गढ़ देता है।

sections.title: Deriving the tilt angle

board_events.text: Deriving tan theta = a / g
Take a fluid element at the surface, mass m.

board_events.caption: Weight, pseudo-force, and the net

<line x1="200" y1="160" x2="200" y2="230" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#b27)"/>
<text x="208" y="215" fill="#22303c" font-size="12">m g</text>
<line x1="200" y1="160" x2="120" y2="160" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#b27)"/>
<text x="120" y="150" fill="#b3402f" font-size="12">m a</text>

<text x="90" y="230" fill="#2f7d5a" font-size="11">net</text>

</svg>

board_events.text: The surface cannot support a force along itself.
So the net of gravity and pseudo-force is perpendicular.
The height gap over length L is a L over g.

segments.text: <curious> Let us derive the tilt angle cleanly from a force balance.
Take a small fluid element right at the free surface, mass m, and work in the accelerating frame.
Two influences act along with the surface force: its weight m g downward, and the pseudo-force m a backward.
Here is the crucial physical point. A fluid surface cannot support any force along itself, because that would make it flow.
So the resultant of gravity and the pseudo-force must be perpendicular to the surface.
That resultant makes an angle theta with the vertical, where tan theta equals m a over m g, which is simply a over g.
<excited> This theta is exactly the tilt from the horizontal, and over a tank of length L the height difference is L tan theta, that is a L over g.
<curious> चलो tilt angle को एक force balance से साफ़-साफ़ derive करते हैं।
Free surface पर एक small fluid element लो, mass m, और accelerating frame में काम करो।
Surface force के साथ दो influences: इसका weight m g नीचे, और pseudo-force m a पीछे।
यहाँ crucial physical point है। Fluid surface अपने साथ किसी force को support नहीं कर सकती, क्योंकि उससे वो flow करने लगेगी।
तो gravity और pseudo-force का resultant surface के perpendicular होना ही चाहिए।
वो resultant vertical से angle theta बनाता है, जहाँ tan theta equals m a over m g, यानी simply a over g।
<excited> यही theta horizontal से tilt है, और length L के tank पर height difference L tan theta, यानी a L over g।

board_events.text: Deriving the paraboloid surface
Take a surface element at radius r; it needs centripetal force.

board_events.caption: Radial gradient supplies the centripetal force
board_events.svg:

<defs><marker id="b28" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto" markerUnits="userSpaceOnUse"><path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 Z" fill="#22303c"/></marker></defs>
<rect x="80" y="60" width="240" height="170" fill="none" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="2"/>
<path d="M80,120 Q200,210 320,120" fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<line x1="200" y1="45" x2="200" y2="230" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
<line x1="200" y1="175" x2="270" y2="147" stroke="#22303c" stroke-width="1.5"/>
<text x="235" y="175" fill="#22303c" font-size="11">r</text>
<circle cx="270" cy="147" r="6" fill="#c2820a"/>
<line x1="270" y1="147" x2="225" y2="147" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#b28)"/>
<text x="235" y="138" fill="#b3402f" font-size="11">centripetal</text>
<text x="200" y="255" text-anchor="middle" fill="#22303c" font-size="12">dP/dr = rho omega squared r, so dy/dr = omega squared r / g</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Along the surface the pressure stays constant.
Integrating a linear gradient gives a parabola.

segments.text: <curious> Now let us derive the paraboloid shape itself.
Consider a fluid element at radial distance r on the surface. Moving in a circle, it needs an inward force equal to its mass times omega squared r.
The only source is the pressure difference across it, so the radial pressure gradient is rho times omega squared r.
That is d P over d r equals rho omega squared r.
Along the free surface the pressure is constant, equal to atmospheric. Moving outward by d r, the pressure would rise, so the surface must climb by d y to cancel it.
Balancing the extra hydrostatic pressure gives d y over d r equals omega squared r over g.
Integrate from the central vertex outward, and the surface height is omega squared r squared over two g. That is a paraboloid.
<excited> The quadratic shape arises because the centripetal demand grows linearly with r, and integrating a linear gradient always yields a parabola.
<curious> अब paraboloid shape को खुद derive करते हैं।
Surface पर radial distance r पर एक fluid element लो। Circle में चलते हुए, उसे inward force चाहिए, इसके mass times omega squared r के बराबर।
एकमात्र source है इसके across का pressure difference, तो radial pressure gradient rho times omega squared r है।
यानी d P over d r equals rho omega squared r।
Free surface पर pressure constant रहता है, atmospheric के बराबर। बाहर d r चलने पर pressure बढ़ता, तो surface को d y चढ़कर उसे cancel करना पड़ता है।
Extra hydrostatic pressure को balance करने से d y over d r equals omega squared r over g मिलता है।
Central vertex से बाहर integrate करो, surface height omega squared r squared over two g है। यही paraboloid है।
<excited> Quadratic shape इसलिए क्योंकि centripetal demand r के साथ linearly बढ़ती है, और linear gradient integrate करने पर हमेशा parabola बनता है।

sections.subtopic: Fluids in Accelerated and Rotating Frames
sections.title: Your accelerated and rotating toolkit

board_events.text: Accelerated and rotating toolkit

board_events.latex: g_{eff} = g \pm a,\quad P = P_0 + \rho(g\pm a)h

board_events.text: Volume conservation: rim rises omega squared R squared over 4 g.
All of fluid statics still holds, just use g_eff.

segments.text: <curious> Let us gather the whole toolkit for accelerated and rotating fluids.
Horizontal acceleration: the tilt is tan theta equals a over g, and the effective gravity is root of a squared plus g squared.
The height difference over a tank of length L is a L over g.
Vertical acceleration: g effective is g plus or minus a, so pressure is P naught plus rho times g plus or minus a, times h.
For rotation, the radial pressure gradient is rho omega squared r.
The surface is a paraboloid, height omega squared r squared over two g, and the rim to centre difference is omega squared R squared over two g.
For a uniform cylinder, volume conservation says the rim rises by omega squared R squared over four g, and the centre falls the same.
<whisper> The master idea for all of it: every fluid-statics result still holds. Just use the effective gravity.
<curious> Accelerated और rotating fluids का पूरा toolkit इकट्ठा कर लेते हैं।
Horizontal acceleration: tilt tan theta equals a over g, और effective gravity root of a squared plus g squared।
Length L के tank पर height difference a L over g।
Vertical acceleration: g effective g plus or minus a, तो pressure P naught plus rho times g plus or minus a, times h।
Rotation के लिए, radial pressure gradient rho omega squared r।
Surface एक paraboloid है, height omega squared r squared over two g, और rim to centre difference omega squared R squared over two g।
Uniform cylinder के लिए, volume conservation कहता है rim omega squared R squared over four g उठता है, और centre उतना ही गिरता है।
<whisper> इस सबका master idea: हर fluid-statics result जस का तस चलता है। बस effective gravity use करो।

sections.subtopic: Fluids in Accelerated and Rotating Frames
sections.title: Diesel tanker: the surface tilt angle

board_events.text: CBSE: diesel tanker tilt
Tanker accelerates at 3.0; find the surface tilt angle.

segments.text: <curious> A clean C B S E problem, a diesel tanker on a straight road.
It accelerates uniformly at three point zero metres per second squared. Find the angle the diesel surface makes with the horizontal.
The surface tilts at an angle theta where tan theta equals a over g.
That is three point zero over ten, which is zero point three zero.
So theta is the inverse tangent of zero point three, about sixteen point seven degrees.
<excited> And the surface rises toward the rear of the tanker.
The diesel lags behind the acceleration, just as you are pushed back into your seat.
<curious> एक साफ़ C B S E problem, सीधी सड़क पर एक diesel tanker।
वो uniformly three point zero metres per second squared पर accelerate करती है। Diesel surface horizontal से कितना angle बनाती है, निकालो।
Surface angle theta पर झुकती है जहाँ tan theta equals a over g।
यानी three point zero over ten, जो zero point three zero है।
तो theta है zero point three का inverse tangent, लगभग sixteen point seven degrees।
<excited> और surface tanker के rear की ओर उठती है।
Diesel acceleration से पीछे रह जाता है, ठीक जैसे तुम अपनी seat में पीछे धकेले जाते हो।

segments.text: <curious> A quick N E E T speed trap that rewards a benchmark.
A beaker of water on a cart tilts so its surface makes forty five degrees with the horizontal. What is the acceleration?
The trap is over-thinking it. The angle depends only on a over g, not on the beaker size or the amount of water.
From tan theta equals a over g, the acceleration is g times tan forty five degrees.
The tangent of forty five degrees is one, so a equals g, which is ten metres per second squared.
<whisper> Anchor this benchmark for good: forty five degrees means a equals g.
A tilt steeper than forty five degrees needs an acceleration greater than g.
<curious> एक झटपट N E E T speed trap जो एक benchmark का इनाम देता है।
एक cart पर beaker का पानी इतना झुकता है कि surface horizontal से forty five degrees बनाती है। Acceleration क्या है?
Trap है over-thinking। Angle सिर्फ a over g पर depend करता है, beaker के size या पानी की quantity पर नहीं।
tan theta equals a over g से, acceleration g times tan forty five degrees है।
Forty five degrees का tangent one है, तो a equals g, यानी ten metres per second squared।
<whisper> इस benchmark को पक्का कर लो: forty five degrees यानी a equals g।
Forty five degrees से steep tilt को g से बड़ा acceleration चाहिए।

segments.text: <curious> A J E E Main problem combining tilt, height gap, and a spill check.
An open tank two metres long holds water one metre deep. The walls are one point two metres tall, and it accelerates along its length at two metres per second squared.
Picture the tilted surface pivoting about the centre of the tank.
First the tilt: tan theta equals a over g, that is two over ten, or zero point two zero.
Over the two-metre length, the end-to-end height difference is two times zero point two, which is zero point four metres.
Now the subtle part: the water pivots about the centre, so it rises by half of that, zero point two metres, at the rear.
The rear level becomes one point zero plus zero point two, that is one point two metres.
<whisper> That exactly reaches the one point two metre wall. On the very verge of spilling, but it does not. Any larger acceleration would spill it.
<curious> एक J E E Main problem जो tilt, height gap, और spill check को जोड़ता है।
एक open tank two metres लंबा, पानी one metre deep। दीवारें one point two metres ऊँची, और वो अपनी length के साथ two metres per second squared पर accelerate करता है।
Tilted surface को tank के centre पर pivot करते सोचो।
पहले tilt: tan theta equals a over g, यानी two over ten, या zero point two zero।
Two metre length पर, end to end height difference two times zero point two, यानी zero point four metres।
अब बारीक बात: पानी centre पर pivot करता है, तो वो उसका आधा, zero point two metres, rear में उठता है।
Rear का level बनता है one point zero plus zero point two, यानी one point two metres।
<whisper> ये ठीक one point two metre दीवार तक पहुँचता है। Spill की बिलकुल कगार पर, पर spill नहीं होता। ज़रा भी ज़्यादा acceleration इसे गिरा देता।

board_events.text: Volume conservation with the vertex at the bottom.
Rim reaches 2H: double the original depth.

segments.text: <curious> A J E E Advanced favourite, a rotating cylinder that bares its own base.
A cylinder of radius ten centimetres holds water twenty centimetres deep at rest. It is spun until the water at the centre just exposes the bottom.
When rotating, the surface is a paraboloid. The vertex sits at the centre, and the rim rises above it.
Apply volume conservation with the centre condition: the vertex is right at the bottom, so its height is zero.
The mean rise equals half the rim height, so omega squared R squared over four g equals H, giving omega equals two over R times root g H.
Substituting, omega is two over zero point one times root of ten times zero point two, which is twenty root two, about twenty eight point three radians per second.
With the vertex at the bottom, the rim height is the full paraboloid depth, omega squared R squared over two g, which is zero point four metres, or forty centimetres.
<excited> Notice the rim reaches twice the original depth. Zero at the centre, forty centimetres at the rim, and the paraboloid average still returns twenty centimetres.
<curious> एक J E E Advanced favourite, एक rotating cylinder जो अपनी ही base खोल देता है।
दस centimetres radius का cylinder rest पर बीस centimetres deep पानी रखता है। इसे तब तक घुमाया जाता है जब centre का पानी just bottom expose कर दे।
घूमते वक़्त surface एक paraboloid है। Vertex centre पर बैठता है, और rim उसके ऊपर उठता है।
Centre condition के साथ volume conservation लगाओ: vertex bottom पर ही है, तो उसकी height zero।
Mean rise rim height का आधा है, तो omega squared R squared over four g equals H, जिससे omega equals two over R times root g H।
Substitute करने पर, omega two over zero point one times root of ten times zero point two, यानी twenty root two, लगभग twenty eight point three radians per second।
Vertex bottom पर होने से, rim height पूरी paraboloid depth है, omega squared R squared over two g, यानी zero point four metres, या forty centimetres।
<excited> ध्यान दो rim original depth का दोगुना पहुँचता है। Centre पर zero, rim पर forty centimetres, और paraboloid average फिर भी twenty centimetres लौटाता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: accelerated and rotating fluids

board_events.text: Pitfalls and pro-tips
Tilt the surface up at the rear, opposite the acceleration.
Volume conservation: add only half the height gap.
Once a fluid accelerates, use g_eff, not g.
Free fall: g_eff = 0, hydrostatic pressure vanishes.
Rim rises omega squared R squared over 4 g, half the total.
Benchmarks: tan theta = a/g, and rim-centre = omega^2 R^2 / 2g.

segments.text: <curious> Let us lock in the traps for accelerated and rotating fluids.
First, tilt direction. Under forward acceleration, the liquid rises at the rear, not the front. Always sketch the pseudo-force pointing opposite the acceleration.
Second, volume conservation. The surface pivots about the centre, so to check spilling, add only half the total height difference at the high end.
Third, use effective gravity. Once a fluid accelerates, every pressure and depth calculation should use g effective, not g.
In free fall, g effective is zero, and hydrostatic pressure vanishes completely.
Fourth, the rotating surface. The rim rises by omega squared R squared over four g relative to the rest level, only half the total rim to centre difference. Do not confuse the two.
<whisper> Memorise the two benchmarks: tan theta equals a over g for tilt, and rim minus centre equals omega squared R squared over two g for spin. Most questions collapse to one line.
<curious> Accelerated और rotating fluids के traps पक्के कर लेते हैं।
पहला, tilt direction। Forward acceleration में liquid rear में उठता है, front में नहीं। Pseudo-force हमेशा acceleration के उल्टा sketch करो।
दूसरा, volume conservation। Surface centre पर pivot करती है, तो spill check के लिए total height difference का सिर्फ आधा high end पर add करो।
तीसरा, effective gravity use करो। एक बार fluid accelerate करे, हर pressure और depth calculation g effective use करे, g नहीं।
Free fall में g effective zero, और hydrostatic pressure पूरी तरह ग़ायब।
चौथा, rotating surface। Rim rest level से omega squared R squared over four g उठता है, यानी total rim to centre difference का सिर्फ आधा। दोनों को मत उलझाओ।
<whisper> दो benchmarks याद रखो: tilt के लिए tan theta equals a over g, और spin के लिए rim minus centre equals omega squared R squared over two g। ज़्यादातर questions एक line में सिमट जाते हैं।

board_events.text: The tangent to a streamline gives the flow direction.
Two streamlines can never cross.
Bundle streamlines into a tube of flow; nothing leaks across.
Push too hard and order dissolves into turbulence.

segments.text: <curious> Stand on a platform as a fast train rushes past, and you feel a tug toward it. That surprise is where we are headed.
But first, how do fluids flow? In steady, or streamline, flow, the velocity at any fixed point never changes with time.
Picture an orderly milk queue through a narrow gate: each particle traces the same path as the one before. That path is a streamline.
The tangent to a streamline gives the flow direction there.
<excited> A crucial property: two streamlines can never cross. If they did, a particle at the crossing would need two velocities at once, which is impossible.
Bundle a set of streamlines together and you get a tube of flow. No fluid leaks across its walls, so whatever enters one end must leave the other.
Push the fluid too hard, though, and the orderly queue dissolves into chaos, eddies and swirls. That is turbulent flow.
<curious> Platform पर खड़े हो और तेज़ train गुज़रे, तो तुम्हें उसकी ओर एक tug महसूस होता है। यही surprise हमारी मंज़िल है।
पर पहले, fluids flow कैसे करते हैं? Steady, यानी streamline, flow में किसी fixed point पर velocity time के साथ कभी नहीं बदलती।
एक व्यवस्थित milk queue सोचो जो narrow gate से गुज़रती है: हर particle पिछले जैसा ही path बनाता है। वही path एक streamline है।
किसी streamline की tangent वहाँ की flow direction देती है।
<excited> एक crucial property: दो streamlines कभी cross नहीं कर सकतीं। अगर करतीं, तो crossing पर particle को एक साथ दो velocities चाहिए होतीं, जो impossible है।
कई streamlines को bundle करो और एक tube of flow बनता है। इसकी walls से कोई fluid leak नहीं होता, तो जो एक सिरे से घुसे वही दूसरे से निकले।
पर fluid को बहुत ज़ोर से धकेलो, तो व्यवस्थित queue chaos में बदल जाती है, eddies और swirls। वही turbulent flow है।

board_events.text: Shrink the area and the speed must rise.
Av is the volume flow rate Q.
A thumb over a hose sends water spraying fast and far.

segments.text: <curious> Consider water flowing through a pipe that narrows, like a garden hose you pinch at the end.
The same amount of water per second must pass through the wide part and the narrow part. Water cannot pile up or vanish.
So in the narrow section, with less room, the water must move faster to keep the throughput constant.
That is the equation of continuity: A one v one equals A two v two.
Shrink the area A, and the speed v shoots up to compensate.
<excited> The product A times v is the volume flow rate Q, measured in cubic metres per second.
Pinch the hose, shrink A, and a thumb over the end sends water spraying fast across the garden.
<curious> एक narrow होते pipe में बहते पानी को सोचो, जैसे garden hose जिसे तुम सिरे पर pinch करते हो।
हर second उतना ही पानी wide और narrow दोनों parts से गुज़रना चाहिए। पानी न इकट्ठा हो सकता है न ग़ायब।
तो narrow section में, कम जगह होने से, throughput constant रखने के लिए पानी को तेज़ चलना पड़ता है।
यही equation of continuity है: A one v one equals A two v two।
Area A घटाओ, और speed v compensate करने के लिए तेज़ी से बढ़ता है।
<excited> Product A times v ही volume flow rate Q है, cubic metres per second में measured।
Hose को pinch करो, A घटाओ, और सिरे पर अंगूठा पानी को garden में दूर तक spray कर देता है।

A flowing fluid carries pressure, kinetic, and potential energy.

board_events.text: The three forms can only shuffle between one another.
On a level pipe, faster flow means lower pressure.
The fast air beside the train spent its pressure to buy speed.

segments.text: <curious> Now we can close the loop on the train mystery. It comes from Daniel Bernoulli.
A flowing fluid carries three kinds of energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy.
Bernoulli theorem is simply energy conservation for a flowing ideal fluid: the sum of these three stays constant along a streamline.
In symbols, P plus half rho v squared plus rho g h is constant.
The energy can only shuffle between the three forms.
<excited> So on a level pipe, if the fluid speeds up and gains kinetic energy, it must pay by dropping its pressure. Faster flow means lower pressure.
The fast air beside the train has spent its pressure to buy speed, so the higher pressure behind you nudges you toward the train.

segments.text: <curious> This single principle explains a startling range of phenomena.
An aeroplane wing: the air travels faster over the curved top, so the pressure there is lower, and the higher pressure below produces a net upward lift.
A perfume atomizer: fast air blown across a tube mouth lowers the pressure and sucks the liquid up.
A spinning cricket ball that swings in flight, through the Magnus effect.
And roofs torn off in a storm: fast wind over the roof lowers the pressure above it, so the higher pressure inside lifts the roof off.
<excited> Every one of these is the same idea: where the fluid moves fast, its pressure is low.
Learn the core relation once, and all of these applications follow from it.
<curious> ये एक ही principle phenomena की एक हैरान करने वाली range समझा देता है।
एक aeroplane wing: हवा curved top पर तेज़ चलती है, तो वहाँ pressure कम, और नीचे का ज़्यादा pressure net upward lift देता है।
एक perfume atomizer: tube के मुँह पर तेज़ हवा pressure गिराती है और liquid को ऊपर खींच लेती है।
एक spinning cricket ball जो हवा में swing करती है, Magnus effect से।
और तूफ़ान में उड़ती छतें: छत के ऊपर तेज़ हवा वहाँ का pressure गिराती है, तो अंदर का ज़्यादा pressure छत को उठा देता है।

segments.text: <curious> Let us derive continuity from simple bookkeeping of volume.
Take steady, incompressible flow through a tube of flow, with no leakage across its walls.
Look at two sections, wide and narrow, and watch a small slug of fluid over a time d t.
At section one, the fluid advances a distance v one d t, so the volume entering is A one v one d t.
Because the fluid is incompressible and cannot accumulate inside the tube, the volume leaving at section two in the same time must be identical.
So A one v one d t equals A two v two d t.
<excited> Cancel the time, and you get A one v one equals A two v two. It is just conservation of mass: narrow the pipe and the fluid speeds up.
<curious> चलो continuity को volume की simple bookkeeping से derive करते हैं।
एक tube of flow से steady, incompressible flow लो, walls के across कोई leakage नहीं।
दो sections देखो, wide और narrow, और एक small fluid slug को time d t पर देखो।
Section one पर fluid distance v one d t आगे बढ़ता है, तो घुसने वाला volume A one v one d t है।
चूँकि fluid incompressible है और tube में इकट्ठा नहीं हो सकता, उसी time में section two से निकलने वाला volume बिल्कुल identical होना चाहिए।
तो A one v one d t equals A two v two d t।
<excited> Time cancel करो, और A one v one equals A two v two मिलता है। ये बस conservation of mass है: pipe narrow करो और fluid तेज़।

board_events.text: Pressure does net work on the slug.
Work-energy theorem, with gravity as the slug rises.

board_events.latex: P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2

segments.text: <curious> Now derive Bernoulli itself, using work and energy.
Assume steady, incompressible, non-viscous, irrotational flow, and follow a slug of fluid between two sections.
As it moves in time d t, a volume delta V enters at section one and an equal delta V emerges at section two.
The fluid behind pushes it in at section one, doing positive work; the fluid ahead pushes back at section two, doing negative work.
The net work by pressure is P one minus P two, times the volume delta V.
By the work-energy theorem, this net work, plus the work of gravity as the slug rises from h one to h two, equals the change in kinetic energy.
Writing that out gives pressure work minus m g times the height change equals the change in half m v squared.
<excited> Substitute mass equals rho delta V, divide through, and rearrange: P plus half rho v squared plus rho g h is the same at both sections. Bernoulli is energy conservation per unit volume.
<curious> अब Bernoulli को खुद derive करते हैं, work और energy से।
मानो steady, incompressible, non-viscous, irrotational flow, और दो sections के बीच एक fluid slug को follow करो।
Time d t में चलते हुए, section one पर volume delta V घुसता है और उतना ही delta V section two पर निकलता है।
पीछे का fluid section one पर इसे धकेलता है, positive work; आगे का fluid section two पर धक्का देता है, negative work।
Pressure का net work P one minus P two, times volume delta V है।
Work-energy theorem से, ये net work, plus slug के h one से h two उठने पर gravity का work, kinetic energy के change के बराबर है।
इसे लिखो तो pressure work minus m g times height change equals half m v squared का change।
<excited> Mass equals rho delta V रखो, divide करो, rearrange करो: P plus half rho v squared plus rho g h दोनों sections पर same। Bernoulli per unit volume energy conservation है।

board_events.text: Same speed as a body falling freely through the depth.

segments.text: <curious> A beautiful special case, Torricelli speed of efflux.
A large open tank is filled to height H, with a small hole punched at height h from the base, that is at depth H minus h below the surface.
Apply Bernoulli between the free surface and the hole.
Both are open to the atmosphere, so those pressures are equal and will cancel.
Because the tank is large, the surface descends very slowly, so the speed at the surface is nearly zero.
Taking the base as datum, P naught plus rho g H equals P naught plus half rho v squared plus rho g h.
The P naught terms cancel, and solving gives the efflux speed, root of two g times H minus h.
<excited> That is exactly the speed of a body falling freely through the depth H minus h. Efflux is free fall in disguise.
<curious> एक ख़ूबसूरत special case, Torricelli speed of efflux।
एक बड़ा open tank height H तक भरा है, base से height h पर एक small hole, यानी surface से depth H minus h नीचे।
Free surface और hole के बीच Bernoulli लगाओ।
दोनों atmosphere के लिए open हैं, तो वो pressures equal हैं और cancel हो जाएँगे।
Tank बड़ा है, इसलिए surface बहुत धीरे उतरता है, तो surface की speed लगभग zero।
Base को datum मानकर, P naught plus rho g H equals P naught plus half rho v squared plus rho g h।
P naught terms cancel हो जाते हैं, और solve करने पर efflux speed मिलती है, root of two g times H minus h।
<excited> ये ठीक उस body की speed है जो depth H minus h से freely गिरे। Efflux असल में free fall है।

board_events.text: The flow toolkit
Continuity first, Bernoulli second.

segments.text: <curious> Let us assemble the whole flow toolkit.
Continuity: A one v one equals A two v two, and that product is the volume flow rate Q. It needs only incompressible, steady flow.
Bernoulli: P plus half rho v squared plus rho g h is constant along a streamline. It needs an ideal fluid.
On a horizontal streamline, static plus dynamic pressure equals the stagnation pressure, a constant.
Torricelli efflux: the speed from a hole is root of two g times H minus h, the depth below the surface.
The horizontal range of that jet is two root h times H minus h, maximum equal to H when the hole is at half the height.
The Reynolds number, rho v D over eta, is dimensionless and predicts the flow type: below about one thousand streamline, above two thousand turbulent.
<whisper> And the master workflow: continuity first to get the speed, Bernoulli second to get the pressure.
<curious> पूरा flow toolkit इकट्ठा कर लेते हैं।
Continuity: A one v one equals A two v two, और वो product volume flow rate Q है। इसे सिर्फ incompressible, steady flow चाहिए।
Bernoulli: P plus half rho v squared plus rho g h एक streamline के साथ constant। इसे एक ideal fluid चाहिए।
Horizontal streamline पर, static plus dynamic pressure equals stagnation pressure, एक constant।
Torricelli efflux: hole से speed root of two g times H minus h है, surface से नीचे की depth।
उस jet का horizontal range two root h times H minus h है, maximum H के बराबर जब hole आधी height पर हो।
Reynolds number, rho v D over eta, dimensionless है और flow type बताता है: लगभग one thousand से नीचे streamline, two thousand से ऊपर turbulent।
<whisper> और master workflow: पहले continuity से speed, फिर Bernoulli से pressure।

segments.text: <curious> A clean C B S E continuity problem, a narrowing pipe.
Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose diameter narrows from six centimetres to two centimetres, entering the wide part at two metres per second.
By continuity, A one v one equals A two v two, and area is proportional to diameter squared.
So the exit speed is the inlet speed times the diameter ratio, all squared.
That is two times six over two, all squared, which is two times nine.
The speed in the narrow section is eighteen metres per second.
<excited> The speed rises ninefold because the diameter shrank threefold, and area depends on diameter squared.

Continuity से, A one v one equals A two v two, और area diameter squared के proportional है।
तो exit speed inlet speed times diameter ratio, all squared है।
यानी two times six over two, all squared, जो two times nine है।
Narrow section में speed eighteen metres per second है।
<excited> Speed नौ गुना बढ़ता है क्योंकि diameter तीन गुना घटा, और area diameter squared पर depend करता है।

segments.text: <curious> A J E E Main problem that chains continuity and Bernoulli.
In the wide section the area is eight square centimetres, the speed three metres per second, and the pressure two times ten to the fifth pascals. The pipe narrows to two square centimetres.
First move, continuity. The exit speed is the inlet speed times the area ratio.
That is three times eight over two, which is twelve metres per second.
Second move, Bernoulli. The pipe is horizontal, so the height terms drop out, leaving static plus dynamic pressure conserved.
So P two equals P one plus half rho times v one squared minus v two squared.
Numerically, two times ten to the fifth plus five hundred times nine minus one hundred forty four, which is one point three two five times ten to the fifth pascals.

segments.text: <curious> A J E E Advanced problem fusing Torricelli with a little calculus.
A cylindrical tank of area one square metre is filled to five metres. A small hole of area one square centimetre opens at the bottom. How long to empty completely?
When the level is at height y, Torricelli gives the efflux speed root of two g y.
The outflow rate at the hole equals the rate at which the stored volume shrinks.
So a times root two g y equals minus A times d y d t. The minus sign is because y is decreasing.
Separate variables and integrate from H down to zero. The emptying time is A over a, times root of two H over g.
Substituting, A over a is ten thousand, and root of two H over g is one second, so the time is ten thousand seconds, about two point eight hours.
<whisper> Notice the time scales as root H, not H, because the outflow slows as the level falls. The huge area ratio is why a small hole drains a big tank so slowly.
<curious> एक J E E Advanced problem जो Torricelli को थोड़े calculus से जोड़ता है।
One square metre area का एक cylindrical tank five metres तक भरा है। नीचे one square centimetre area का एक small hole खुलता है। पूरा खाली होने में कितना समय?

Hole पर outflow rate उतना ही है जितनी तेज़ी से stored volume घटता है।
तो a times root two g y equals minus A times d y d t। Minus sign इसलिए क्योंकि y घट रहा है।
Variables separate करो और H से zero तक integrate करो। Emptying time A over a, times root of two H over g है।
Substitute करने पर, A over a ten thousand है, और root of two H over g one second, तो time ten thousand seconds, लगभग two point eight hours।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: flow and Bernoulli

board_events.text: Pitfalls and pro-tips
Fast fluid means low pressure, never high.
Bernoulli needs an ideal fluid along a single streamline.
Efflux uses the depth of the hole below the surface.
Volume flow rate Q is conserved; the speed v is not.
Continuity first, Bernoulli second.
Shortcut: efflux speed equals free-fall speed through the depth.

segments.text: <curious> Let us lock in the flow traps, and the first is the big one.

Fast fluid equals high pressure is the most damaging misconception in the chapter. Bernoulli says the opposite on a level streamline: faster flow means lower static pressure, because kinetic energy is bought at the cost of pressure energy.
Second, Bernoulli needs an ideal fluid, non-viscous, incompressible, steady, irrotational, along a single streamline. For turbulent or viscous flow it fails.
Third, efflux uses the depth of the hole below the free surface, not the tank full height and not the hole height above the ground.
Fourth, do not confuse volume flow rate with speed. Q equals A v is conserved through a pipe; the speed v is not, since it changes as the area changes.
The pro-workflow: continuity first to hand you the unknown speed, then Bernoulli to get the pressure.
<whisper> And the shortcut worth keeping: efflux speed equals free-fall speed through the depth, root of two g delta h.
<curious> Flow के traps पक्के कर लेते हैं, और पहला सबसे बड़ा है।

Fast fluid equals high pressure इस chapter की सबसे नुक़सानदेह misconception है। Bernoulli level streamline पर उल्टा कहता है: तेज़ flow यानी कम static pressure, क्योंकि kinetic energy pressure energy की क़ीमत पर ख़रीदी जाती है।
दूसरा, Bernoulli को एक ideal fluid चाहिए, non-viscous, incompressible, steady, irrotational, एक single streamline के साथ। Turbulent या viscous flow के लिए ये fail होता है।
तीसरा, efflux hole की free surface से नीचे की depth use करता है, न tank की full height, न ground से hole की height।
चौथा, volume flow rate को speed से मत उलझाओ। Q equals A v pipe में conserved है; speed v नहीं, क्योंकि area बदलते ही वो बदलता है।
Pro-workflow: पहले continuity से unknown speed, फिर Bernoulli से pressure।
<whisper> और रखने लायक shortcut: efflux speed depth से free-fall speed के बराबर, root of two g delta h।

segments.text: <curious> Pour out water and it splashes away. Tip up honey and it crawls down in a slow, lazy ribbon.
Both are fluids, both flow, but honey resists flowing far more. That internal resistance is viscosity, fluid friction.
Picture a deep river. The water at the bed is essentially stuck; the surface moves fastest; each layer in between slides over the one below.
So each thin horizontal layer moves a little faster than its neighbour beneath and a little slower than the one above.
This smooth, layered sliding sets up a velocity gradient, the change in speed per unit distance across the flow, written d v over d x.
Newton found the viscous force is proportional to the contact area and to the velocity gradient: F equals minus eta A times d v over d x.
<excited> The negative sign is the signature of friction: the force always opposes the relative motion, dragging the fluid toward uniformity.
The constant eta is the coefficient of viscosity, large for honey, small for water, and tinier still for air.
<curious> पानी उँडेलो तो छपाक से बिखर जाता है। शहद झुकाओ तो धीमी, आलसी लकीर में रेंगता है।
दोनों fluids हैं, दोनों flow करते हैं, पर शहद flow का कहीं ज़्यादा resist करता है। वही internal resistance है viscosity, fluid friction।
एक गहरी नदी सोचो। Bed का पानी लगभग अटका है; surface सबसे तेज़ चलता है; बीच की हर layer नीचे वाली पर slide करती है।
तो हर पतली horizontal layer नीचे वाली से थोड़ी तेज़ और ऊपर वाली से थोड़ी धीमी चलती है।
यही smooth, layered sliding एक velocity gradient बनाती है, flow के across per unit distance speed का change, यानी d v over d x।
Newton ने पाया viscous force contact area और velocity gradient के proportional है: F equals minus eta A times d v over d x।
<excited> Negative sign friction की पहचान है: force हमेशा relative motion का विरोध करती है, fluid को uniformity की ओर खींचती है।
Constant eta ही coefficient of viscosity है, शहद के लिए बड़ा, पानी के लिए छोटा, और हवा के लिए और भी tiny।

segments.text: <curious> Here is a fact examiners love, and it splits oppositely for liquids and gases.
Heat a liquid, warm honey say, and it flows more easily. Its viscosity falls.
The reason: heat weakens the cohesive bonds between liquid molecules, so the layers slide past each other more freely.
So for liquids, viscosity decreases as temperature rises, roughly as one over the temperature.
For a gas the opposite happens. Heat it and it becomes more viscous.
<excited> Gas viscosity arises from molecular diffusion between layers, which intensifies on heating, so it rises with temperature.
Getting this split backwards is the classic error here. Liquids loosen, gases gum up.
<curious> ये एक fact examiners को बहुत पसंद है, और liquids और gases के लिए उल्टा बँटता है।
एक liquid को गरम करो, जैसे गरम शहद, तो वो आसानी से flow करता है। इसकी viscosity गिरती है।
कारण: heat liquid molecules के cohesive bonds को कमज़ोर करती है, तो layers एक दूसरे पर ज़्यादा freely slide करती हैं।
तो liquids के लिए, temperature बढ़ते ही viscosity घटती है, लगभग one over temperature की तरह।
एक gas के लिए उल्टा होता है। इसे गरम करो और ये ज़्यादा viscous हो जाती है।
<excited> Gas viscosity layers के बीच molecular diffusion से आती है, जो गरम करने पर तेज़ होती है, तो ये temperature के साथ बढ़ती है।
इस split को उल्टा करना यहाँ की classic ग़लती है। Liquids loosen, gases gum up।

segments.text: <curious> Now apply viscosity to a small object falling through a fluid.
Think of a steel pellet sinking in glycerine, or a raindrop falling through air.
Three forces act: its weight pulling down, the buoyant force pushing up, and the viscous drag pushing up against its motion.
The weight is fixed, but the drag is special: it grows with speed.
So as the object speeds up, the upward drag grows until, at some speed, the three forces exactly balance.
<excited> At that instant the net force is zero, acceleration stops, and the speed becomes constant, the terminal velocity.
This is why a raindrop does not hit you at bullet speed despite falling kilometres, and why cloud droplets seem to hang in the air.

Weight fixed है, पर drag ख़ास है: वो speed के साथ बढ़ता है।
तो जैसे object तेज़ होता है, upward drag बढ़ता है जब तक किसी speed पर तीनों forces बिल्कुल balance न हो जाएँ।
<excited> उस पल net force zero होती है, acceleration रुकती है, और speed constant हो जाती है, terminal velocity।

segments.text: <curious> A clean C B S E problem, dragging a plate over glycerine.
A flat plate of area zero point one square metres rests on a glycerine layer two millimetres thick, and is dragged at a steady half a metre per second. The viscosity is one point five pascal seconds.
Assume a uniform velocity gradient, with the glycerine touching the table stationary.
The velocity gradient is the top speed minus zero, over the gap.
That is zero point five over two times ten to the minus three, which is two hundred fifty per second.
The force needed balances the viscous force, eta A times the gradient, one point five times zero point one times two hundred fifty.
<excited> That gives thirty seven point five newtons, the tangential force to keep the plate moving steadily.
<curious> एक साफ़ C B S E problem, glycerine पर एक plate खींचना।
Zero point one square metres area की एक flat plate two millimetres मोटी glycerine layer पर रखी है, और steady आधा metre per second पर खींची जाती है। Viscosity one point five pascal seconds।
एक uniform velocity gradient मानो, table को छूता glycerine stationary।
Velocity gradient है top speed minus zero, gap के ऊपर।
यानी zero point five over two times ten to the minus three, जो two hundred fifty per second है।
ज़रूरी force viscous force को balance करती है, eta A times gradient, one point five times zero point one times two hundred fifty।
<excited> ये देता है thirty seven point five newtons, plate को steadily चलाने की tangential force।

board_events.text: Terminal velocity scales as r squared, not r or volume.
8 droplets means radius halves, so speed quarters.

segments.text: <curious> A quick N E E T trap that rewards the correct scaling.
A raindrop of radius r falls at terminal velocity v. It breaks into eight identical smaller droplets. Find the new terminal velocity.
The traps: do not scale with radius, giving v over two, or with volume, giving v over eight. It scales as r squared.
First find the new radius from volume conservation, since the volume is unchanged when the drop splits.
Four thirds pi r cubed equals eight times four thirds pi r prime cubed, so r prime cubed is r cubed over eight, and r prime is r over two.
Now use terminal velocity proportional to r squared. The new speed is v times one half squared, which is v over four.
<excited> Eight droplets means the radius halves, and since terminal velocity goes as r squared, the speed quarters. Fine mist lingers while big drops plummet.
<curious> एक झटपट N E E T trap जो सही scaling का इनाम देता है।
Radius r का एक raindrop terminal velocity v पर गिरता है। वो आठ identical छोटे droplets में टूटता है। नई terminal velocity निकालो।
Traps: radius के साथ मत scale करो, जो v over two देता है, न volume के साथ, जो v over eight। ये r squared के साथ scale करता है।
पहले volume conservation से नया radius निकालो, क्योंकि drop टूटने पर volume unchanged रहता है।
Four thirds pi r cubed equals eight times four thirds pi r prime cubed, तो r prime cubed r cubed over eight, और r prime r over two।
अब terminal velocity proportional to r squared use करो। नई speed v times one half squared, यानी v over four।
<excited> आठ droplets यानी radius आधा, और terminal velocity r squared के साथ, तो speed चौथाई। बारीक mist टिकी रहती है जबकि बड़े drops गिर पड़ते हैं।
