board_events.text: Drag equals apparent weight: the balance confirmed.

segments.text: <curious> A J E E Main problem that reuses buoyancy and Stokes drag together.
A glass sphere of radius two millimetres and density two thousand five hundred falls through glycerine of density one thousand two hundred sixty and viscosity zero point eight three.
Find the terminal velocity, the drag at terminal velocity, and verify it equals the apparent weight.
The terminal velocity is two ninths r squared times the density difference times g, over eta, about one point three three times ten to the minus two metres per second.
The Stokes drag at that speed is six pi eta r times v terminal, about four point one six times ten to the minus four newtons.
The apparent weight, effective weight minus buoyancy, is four thirds pi r cubed times the density difference times g, also about four point one six times ten to the minus four newtons.
<excited> The two match exactly, confirming the force balance: at terminal velocity, the drag supports the sphere against its buoyancy-reduced weight.
<curious> एक J E E Main problem जो buoyancy और Stokes drag साथ दोबारा इस्तेमाल करता है।
Radius two millimetres और density two thousand five hundred की glass sphere glycerine में गिरती है, जिसकी density one thousand two hundred sixty और viscosity zero point eight three है।
Terminal velocity, terminal velocity पर drag, और verify करो कि वो apparent weight के बराबर है।
Terminal velocity two ninths r squared times density difference times g, over eta है, लगभग one point three three times ten to the minus two metres per second।
उस speed पर Stokes drag six pi eta r times v terminal है, लगभग four point one six times ten to the minus four newtons।
Apparent weight, effective weight minus buoyancy, four thirds pi r cubed times density difference times g है, वो भी लगभग four point one six times ten to the minus four newtons।
<excited> दोनों बिल्कुल match करते हैं, force balance confirm करते हुए: terminal velocity पर drag sphere को उसके buoyancy-घटे weight के ख़िलाफ़ थामता है।

board_events.text: Double the radius, thirty-two times the heating.

segments.text: <curious> A J E E Advanced scaling argument, and it is a beautiful one.
At terminal velocity the sphere moves at constant speed, so all the work against drag becomes heat. The power equals the drag force times the speed.
Track how each factor carries a power of r.
The power is six pi eta r times v terminal squared.
Substitute the terminal velocity. Its square is four eighty firsts r to the fourth times the density difference squared times g squared, over eta squared.
Multiply through, and the power is eight twenty sevenths r to the fifth times the density difference squared g squared over eta, proportional to r to the fifth.
<excited> The chain is transparent: drag as r, terminal speed as r squared, power as r times r to the fourth. Doubling the radius means thirty two times the heating.
<curious> एक J E E Advanced scaling argument, और ये बड़ा ख़ूबसूरत है।
Terminal velocity पर sphere constant speed पर चलती है, तो drag के ख़िलाफ़ सारा work heat बनता है। Power drag force times speed के बराबर है।
देखो हर factor r की एक power कैसे साथ लाता है।
Power six pi eta r times v terminal squared है।
Terminal velocity substitute करो। इसका square four eighty firsts r to the fourth times density difference squared times g squared, over eta squared है।
Multiply करो, और power eight twenty sevenths r to the fifth times density difference squared g squared over eta है, proportional to r to the fifth।
<excited> Chain साफ़ है: drag r के रूप में, terminal speed r squared, power r times r to the fourth। Radius दोगुना यानी बत्तीस गुना heating।

board_events.text: Pitfalls and pro-tips
Liquids get less viscous when heated; gases get more.
Terminal velocity goes as r squared, not r or r cubed.
The driving term is the density difference, not the body alone.
For a bubble, the term is negative, so it rises.
1 poise = 0.1 Pa s; convert before substituting.
Write the three-force balance as your first line.

segments.text: <curious> Let us lock in the viscosity traps.
First, and the classic: liquids get less viscous when heated, gases get more. Anchor it physically: warm honey pours easily, but a hot gas mixes faster between layers.
Second, mis-scaling terminal velocity. It goes as r squared, not r and not r cubed. When a drop splits or coalesces, first find the new radius from volume conservation, then square the ratio.
Third, the driving term is the effective weight, the density difference, not the body density alone. Forgetting buoyancy overestimates the terminal velocity.
For an air bubble in water the density difference is negative, so the term is negative and the bubble rises, which the formula correctly predicts.
Fourth, units: one poise is zero point one pascal seconds, and one decapoise is ten poise. Always convert poise to pascal seconds before substituting, or you will be off by a factor of ten.
<whisper> And the pro-tip: for any falling-sphere problem, write the three-force balance, weight, buoyancy, drag, as your very first line. Every result flows from it.
<curious> Viscosity के traps पक्के कर लेते हैं।
पहला, और classic: liquids गरम होने पर कम viscous, gases ज़्यादा। Physically anchor करो: गरम शहद आसानी से बहता है, पर गरम gas layers के बीच तेज़ mix करती है।
दूसरा, terminal velocity की mis-scaling। ये r squared के साथ जाती है, न r न r cubed। Drop टूटे या मिले, पहले volume conservation से नया radius, फिर ratio का square।
तीसरा, driving term effective weight है, density difference, अकेली body density नहीं। Buoyancy भूलने से terminal velocity ज़्यादा आ जाती है।
पानी में air bubble के लिए density difference negative है, तो term negative और bubble ऊपर उठता है, जो formula सही predict करता है।
चौथा, units: one poise zero point one pascal seconds, और one decapoise ten poise। Substitute से पहले हमेशा poise को pascal seconds में convert करो, वरना factor of ten से off हो जाओगे।
<whisper> और pro-tip: किसी भी falling-sphere problem में, three-force balance, weight, buoyancy, drag, अपनी पहली line में लिखो। हर result उसी से निकलता है।

board_events.text: Longer tube, less flow; more viscous fluid, less flow.
A more viscous fluid also lowers the flow.
Flow depends on radius to the fourth power.
Halve the radius and the flow falls to one sixteenth.

segments.text: <curious> In the last subtopic a sphere fell through still fluid. Now flip it: hold the container still and push the fluid through a thin tube.
Water through a drip pipe, blood through an artery, ink through a pen nib. How fast does it flow? That is what Poiseuille, a physician studying blood, answered.
Think about what limits the flow. Push harder, a bigger pressure difference, and more flows, like opening a tap wider.
Use a longer tube and the flow drops, because the fluid fights viscous drag over a greater distance.
Use a more viscous fluid, honey instead of water, and flow drops, because internal friction is higher.
<excited> But the fourth factor is the shocker: the flow depends on the tube radius raised to the fourth power. Not r, not r squared, but r to the fourth.
Halving a tube radius cuts the flow to one sixteenth, since two to the fourth is sixteen. That is why a tiny arterial narrowing chokes blood flow so dramatically.
<curious> पिछले subtopic में एक sphere still fluid में गिरी थी। अब उलटो: container को still रखो और fluid को एक thin tube से बहाओ।
Drip pipe में पानी, artery में blood, nib में ink। ये कितनी तेज़ बहता है? यही Poiseuille ने, blood पढ़ने वाले एक physician ने, जवाब दिया।
सोचो flow को क्या limit करता है। ज़्यादा ज़ोर से push करो, बड़ा pressure difference, और ज़्यादा बहता है, जैसे tap ज़्यादा खोलना।
Longer tube use करो और flow गिरता है, क्योंकि fluid को ज़्यादा distance पर viscous drag से लड़ना पड़ता है।
ज़्यादा viscous fluid use करो, पानी की जगह शहद, और flow गिरता है, क्योंकि internal friction ज़्यादा है।
<excited> पर चौथा factor चौंकाने वाला है: flow tube के radius की fourth power पर depend करता है। न r, न r squared, बल्कि r to the fourth।
Radius आधा करो और flow one sixteenth रह जाता है, क्योंकि two to the fourth sixteen है। इसीलिए artery का ज़रा सा narrowing blood flow को इतना दबा देता है।

board_events.text: Why radius to the fourth
A wider tube has more area, one factor of r squared.

board_events.text: The core is far from the sticky walls, so it moves faster.
That average-speed boost gives another factor of r squared.
Area times average speed gives radius to the fourth.

segments.text: <curious> Why r to the fourth and not just the cross-sectional area, r squared? Two effects multiply.
First, a wider tube has more cross-sectional area for fluid to pass through. That is one factor of r squared.
Second, and less obvious: in a wider tube, the fluid in the middle is much farther from the sticky walls.
The walls grip the outer layers, but the core slides freely, so on average the fluid moves faster.
This average-speed boost contributes another factor of r squared.
Multiply them, area times average speed, and you get r squared times r squared, which is r to the fourth.
<excited> So the radius matters enormously. A slightly clogged fuel line starves an engine, and arterial plaque is dangerous out of all proportion to its size.
<curious> r to the fourth क्यों, सिर्फ cross-sectional area, r squared क्यों नहीं? दो effects गुणा होते हैं।
पहला, wider tube में fluid के गुज़रने के लिए ज़्यादा cross-sectional area होता है। वो एक factor of r squared है।
दूसरा, और कम obvious: wider tube में बीच का fluid sticky walls से कहीं दूर होता है।
Walls बाहरी layers को पकड़ती हैं, पर core freely slide करता है, तो average में fluid तेज़ चलता है।
ये average-speed boost एक और factor of r squared देता है।
इन्हें गुणा करो, area times average speed, और r squared times r squared मिलता है, जो r to the fourth है।
<excited> तो radius बहुत मायने रखता है। ज़रा सी clogged fuel line engine को भूखा रखती है, और arterial plaque अपने size से कहीं ज़्यादा ख़तरनाक है।

board_events.text: Speed rises from zero at the wall to a maximum at the axis.
Plotted across the tube, it traces a bullet-shaped parabola.
The average speed is exactly half the maximum.
This half-average is used in every flow-rate calculation.

segments.text: <curious> The flow across a viscous tube is not uniform. Let us see its shape.
The fluid touching the wall is essentially stuck, held by what we call the no-slip condition.
Meanwhile the fluid at the centre, the axis, races ahead.
So the speed varies smoothly, from zero at the wall to a maximum at the axis.
Plotted across the tube, it traces a parabolic velocity profile, a bullet-shaped front.
<excited> And a clean result: the average speed turns out to be exactly half the maximum, centre speed.
That half-average is what you use whenever you compute the flow rate as average speed times area.
<curious> एक viscous tube के across flow uniform नहीं होता। इसका shape देखते हैं।
Wall को छूता fluid लगभग अटका है, जिसे हम no-slip condition कहते हैं, उससे थमा।
उधर centre का, axis का fluid आगे दौड़ता है।
तो speed smoothly बदलती है, wall पर zero से axis पर maximum तक।
Tube के across plot करो तो ये एक parabolic velocity profile बनाती है, एक bullet जैसा front।
<excited> और एक साफ़ result: average speed ठीक maximum, यानी centre speed का आधा निकलती है।
यही half-average तुम तब use करते हो जब flow rate को average speed times area के रूप में निकालते हो।

Series: resistances add. Parallel: reciprocals add.
The analogy is quantitative, not just a metaphor.

segments.text: <curious> There is a beautiful unifying idea here, an analogy with electric current.
A pressure difference drives a volume flow through a tube, just as a voltage drives a current through a wire.
The tube resists the flow, so define a fluid resistance, pressure difference over flow rate.
That resistance is eight eta l over pi r to the fourth, perfectly analogous to Ohm's law.
Pressure difference plays the role of voltage, flow rate the role of current, and R the role of resistance.
The rules for combining tubes follow: in series the resistances add, in parallel their reciprocals add, exactly like resistors.
<excited> And this analogy is not a loose metaphor. It works quantitatively, turning any multi-tube network into a familiar circuit problem.
<curious> यहाँ एक ख़ूबसूरत unifying idea है, electric current से एक analogy।
एक pressure difference tube में volume flow चलाता है, ठीक जैसे voltage एक wire में current चलाता है।
Tube flow को resist करता है, तो एक fluid resistance define करो, pressure difference over flow rate।
वो resistance eight eta l over pi r to the fourth है, Ohm's law के perfectly analogous।
Pressure difference voltage का role निभाता है, flow rate current का, और R resistance का।
Tubes जोड़ने के rules निकलते हैं: series में resistances add, parallel में उनके reciprocals add, बिल्कुल resistors की तरह।
<excited> और ये analogy कोई ढीली metaphor नहीं। ये quantitatively काम करती है, किसी भी multi-tube network को एक जाने-पहचाने circuit problem में बदल देती है।

board_events.text: Deriving the profile and the pi over 8
Take a coaxial fluid cylinder of radius s inside the tube.

board_events.text: Sum thin annular rings to get the flow rate.

segments.text: <curious> Now derive both the profile and the mysterious factor pi over eight.
Consider a coaxial fluid cylinder of radius s inside the tube, length l, in steady flow.
Two forces balance on it: the net pressure force pushing it forward, and the viscous drag from the slower fluid just outside.
Setting them equal gives delta P pi s squared equals minus eta times two pi s l times d v d s.
Integrate outward to the wall, where the speed is zero, and you get the parabolic profile: v of s equals delta P over four eta l, times r squared minus s squared.
Now sum the contributions of thin annular rings across the cross-section to get the total flow rate.
<excited> The integral delivers Poiseuille law with the constant pi over eight: Q equals pi delta P r to the fourth, over eight eta l. And the mean speed is exactly half the axial maximum.
<curious> अब profile और वो रहस्यमय factor pi over eight, दोनों derive करते हैं।
Tube के अंदर radius s का एक coaxial fluid cylinder लो, length l, steady flow में।
इस पर दो forces balance होती हैं: आगे धकेलती net pressure force, और बाहर के धीमे fluid से viscous drag।
इन्हें equal रखने से delta P pi s squared equals minus eta times two pi s l times d v d s।
Wall तक बाहर integrate करो, जहाँ speed zero है, और parabolic profile मिलता है: v of s equals delta P over four eta l, times r squared minus s squared।
अब cross-section के thin annular rings के contributions जोड़ो ताकि total flow rate मिले।
<excited> Integral Poiseuille law को constant pi over eight के साथ देता है: Q equals pi delta P r to the fourth, over eight eta l। और mean speed axial maximum का ठीक आधा है।

sections.subtopic: Poiseuille's Law and Viscous Flow Resistance
sections.title: Your Poiseuille toolkit

board_events.text: The Poiseuille toolkit
Scalings: Q goes as delta P, r to the fourth, 1/l, and 1/eta.
Valid only for steady, laminar, Newtonian flow.

segments.text: <curious> Let us gather the Poiseuille toolkit.
Poiseuille law: the flow rate is pi delta P r to the fourth, over eight eta l, for laminar flow through a capillary.
The scalings: flow goes as the pressure difference, as r to the fourth, and inversely as the length and the viscosity.
Fluid resistance is delta P over Q, equal to eight eta l over pi r to the fourth.
Tubes combine like resistors: in series the resistances add, in parallel the reciprocals add.
The velocity profile is parabolic, delta P over four eta l times r squared minus s squared, and the mean speed is half the maximum.
The critical velocity for the onset of turbulence is the Reynolds number times eta, over rho D, where D is the diameter.
<whisper> And remember the fine print: all of this is valid only for steady, laminar, incompressible, Newtonian flow in a long uniform tube.
<curious> Poiseuille toolkit इकट्ठा कर लेते हैं।
Poiseuille law: flow rate pi delta P r to the fourth, over eight eta l है, capillary में laminar flow के लिए।
Scalings: flow pressure difference और r to the fourth के साथ, और length तथा viscosity के inversely जाता है।
Fluid resistance delta P over Q है, eight eta l over pi r to the fourth के बराबर।
Tubes resistors की तरह combine होते हैं: series में resistances add, parallel में reciprocals add।
Velocity profile parabolic है, delta P over four eta l times r squared minus s squared, और mean speed maximum का आधा।
Turbulence शुरू होने की critical velocity Reynolds number times eta, over rho D है, जहाँ D diameter है।
<whisper> और fine print याद रखो: ये सब सिर्फ steady, laminar, incompressible, Newtonian flow के लिए valid है, एक long uniform tube में।

segments.text: <curious> A direct C B S E flow-rate calculation.

Water flows through a horizontal capillary of length zero point two metres and radius zero point five millimetres, under a pressure difference of one thousand pascals. The viscosity is ten to the minus three pascal seconds.
Apply Poiseuille law directly to this capillary.
Flow rate is pi delta P r to the fourth, over eight eta l.
The tricky bit is r to the fourth. Zero point five millimetres is five times ten to the minus four metres, and its fourth power is six point two five times ten to the minus fourteen.
Substituting, the flow rate comes out about one point two three times ten to the minus seven cubic metres per second.
<excited> That is roughly zero point one two millilitres per second, a slow trickle from so fine a tube.

पानी एक horizontal capillary से बहता है, length zero point two metres और radius zero point five millimetres, pressure difference one thousand pascals के तहत। Viscosity ten to the minus three pascal seconds।
इस capillary पर Poiseuille law सीधे लगाओ।
Flow rate pi delta P r to the fourth, over eight eta l है।
मुश्किल हिस्सा r to the fourth है। Zero point five millimetres five times ten to the minus four metres है, और इसकी fourth power six point two five times ten to the minus fourteen।
Substitute करने पर, flow rate लगभग one point two three times ten to the minus seven cubic metres per second आता है।
<excited> ये लगभग zero point one two millilitres per second है, इतनी fine tube से एक धीमी trickle।

segments.text: <curious> A quick N E E T trap, and it tests one fact hard.
A liquid flows through a capillary at rate Q. A second tube of the same length but half the radius is used, under the same pressure difference. Find the new flow rate.
Picture the two tubes, radius r and radius r over two.
The trap: do not scale with area, giving Q over four, or with radius, giving Q over two.
Poiseuille scales as r to the fourth, so the new flow is Q times one half to the fourth.
One half to the fourth is one sixteenth, so the new flow rate is Q over sixteen.
<excited> Radius to the fourth: halving the radius drops the flow sixteenfold. This extreme sensitivity is the whole point of the law.
<curious> एक झटपट N E E T trap, और ये एक fact को कड़ाई से टेस्ट करता है।
एक liquid capillary से rate Q पर बहता है। same length पर पर आधे radius की दूसरी tube use होती है, same pressure difference पर। नया flow rate निकालो।
दोनों tubes सोचो, radius r और radius r over two।
Trap: area के साथ मत scale करो, जो Q over four देता है, न radius के साथ, जो Q over two।
Poiseuille r to the fourth के साथ scale करता है, तो नया flow Q times one half to the fourth है।
One half to the fourth one sixteenth है, तो नया flow rate Q over sixteen।
<excited> Radius to the fourth: radius आधा करने से flow sixteen गुना गिरता है। यही extreme sensitivity इस law की पूरी बात है।

board_events.text: Almost all the drop falls across the narrow tube.

segments.text: <curious> A J E E Main problem on tubes in series, using the resistance analogy.
Two capillaries are joined end to end. The first has radius r, the second radius two r, both the same length l, with a pressure difference across the pair.
In series, add the resistances. Since resistance goes as one over r to the fourth, the wide tube has one sixteenth the resistance of the narrow one.
So the equivalent resistance is R one plus R one over sixteen, that is seventeen sixteenths of R one.
The overall flow is the pressure difference over the equivalent resistance, which tidies to two pi r to the fourth delta P, over seventeen eta l.
The pressure drop across the narrow tube is Q times R one, which is sixteen seventeenths of the total, about ninety four percent.

<excited> Almost the entire pressure drop, sixteen out of seventeen, occurs across the narrow tube. The wide tube barely resists, just as the larger resistor takes the larger voltage share in a series circuit.
<curious> Series में tubes पर एक J E E Main problem, resistance analogy से।
दो capillaries end to end जुड़ी हैं। पहली का radius r, दूसरी का radius two r, दोनों same length l, pair के across एक pressure difference।
Series में resistances जोड़ो। चूँकि resistance one over r to the fourth के साथ जाता है, wide tube की resistance narrow की one sixteenth है।
तो equivalent resistance R one plus R one over sixteen है, यानी R one का seventeen sixteenths।
Overall flow pressure difference over equivalent resistance है, जो two pi r to the fourth delta P, over seventeen eta l बनता है।
Narrow tube के across pressure drop Q times R one है, जो total का sixteen seventeenths, लगभग ninety four percent।
<excited> लगभग पूरा pressure drop, सत्रह में से सोलह, narrow tube के across होता है। Wide tube मुश्किल से resist करता है, जैसे series circuit में बड़ा resistor बड़ा voltage हिस्सा लेता है।

Picture the parabola, fastest at the axis, zero at the walls.
From the profile, the maximum, axial speed is delta P r squared over four eta l.

sections.subtopic: Poiseuille's Law and Viscous Flow Resistance
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: Poiseuille flow

board_events.text: Pitfalls and pro-tips
Flow goes as radius to the fourth, not r squared or r cubed.
Series: resistances add. Parallel: reciprocals add.
Poiseuille holds for laminar flow only; check the Reynolds number.
Mean speed is half the maximum; use the mean for flow rate.
Lean on ratios: Q goes as delta P r^4 over eta l.
Pressure is voltage, flow is current, R = 8 eta l / pi r^4.

segments.text: <curious> Let us lock in the Poiseuille traps.
First, and by far the biggest: flow goes as r to the fourth, not r squared, the area, and not r cubed, the volume. When a problem changes the radius, raise the ratio to the fourth power.
Second, combining tubes. Fluid resistances add in series and reciprocal-add in parallel, exactly like resistors. The narrow tube dominates a series combination.
Third, Poiseuille law is for laminar flow only. Check the Reynolds number first; above about two thousand the flow turns turbulent and the simple scaling fails.
Fourth, do not confuse mean and maximum speed. The centre-line speed is the maximum; the mean, used in flow rate equals mean speed times area, is half of it.
The pro-tip: for any change-the-tube question, lean on the scaling, Q goes as delta P r to the fourth over eta l, and work with ratios, so you rarely need the messy constants.

<whisper> And memorise the resistance analogy: pressure difference is voltage, flow rate is current, resistance is eight eta l over pi r to the fourth. Every network becomes a circuit you already know.
<curious> Poiseuille के traps पक्के कर लेते हैं।
पहला, और अब तक सबसे बड़ा: flow r to the fourth के साथ जाता है, न r squared, area, न r cubed, volume। Problem radius बदले तो ratio को fourth power तक उठाओ।
दूसरा, tubes जोड़ना। Fluid resistances series में add और parallel में reciprocal-add, बिल्कुल resistors की तरह। Series combination में narrow tube हावी रहता है।
तीसरा, Poiseuille law सिर्फ laminar flow के लिए है। पहले Reynolds number check करो; लगभग two thousand से ऊपर flow turbulent हो जाता है और simple scaling fail।
चौथा, mean और maximum speed को मत उलझाओ। Centre-line speed maximum है; mean, जो flow rate equals mean speed times area में आता है, उसका आधा।
Pro-tip: किसी भी change-the-tube question में scaling पर टिको, Q delta P r to the fourth over eta l के साथ जाता है, और ratios से काम करो, तो messy constants शायद ही चाहिए।
<whisper> और resistance analogy याद रखो: pressure difference voltage, flow rate current, resistance eight eta l over pi r to the fourth। हर network एक जाने-पहचाने circuit में बदल जाता है।

A water strider skates; a steel needle floats.

board_events.text: Interior molecules are pulled equally in all directions.
A surface molecule has liquid below but only air above.
With no neighbours pulling up, it feels a net inward pull.
The surface is squeezed taut, so liquids minimise area.
A free drop pulls itself into a sphere: least area.

segments.text: <curious> Watch a water strider skate across a pond, or a sewing needle float on water though steel is denser.
Rain beads into near-perfect spheres on a waxed car, and water climbs a cotton wick against gravity. All trace to one property: surface tension.
It is the tendency of a liquid surface to behave like a stretched elastic membrane, always trying to shrink to the smallest area.
Where does this skin come from? A molecule deep inside is pulled equally in all directions, so the net force on it is zero.
But a molecule right at the surface has liquid below and beside it, and only air above.
<excited> With no neighbours pulling up, it feels a net inward pull. Every surface molecule is tugged toward the bulk.
So the surface is squeezed taut, like the skin of a drum, and liquids minimise their surface area.
A free drop, with no other constraint, pulls itself into a sphere, because a sphere has the least surface area for a given volume.
<curious> एक water strider को तालाब पर फिसलते देखो, या steel के denser होने के बावजूद एक सुई को पानी पर तैरते।
Waxed car पर बारिश लगभग perfect spheres बनाती है, और पानी gravity के ख़िलाफ़ cotton wick पर चढ़ता है। सब एक ही property से: surface tension।
ये एक liquid surface की प्रवृत्ति है कि वो एक stretched elastic membrane जैसा बर्ताव करे, हमेशा सबसे छोटे area तक सिकुड़ने की कोशिश में।
ये skin कहाँ से आती है? अंदर गहराई में एक molecule हर direction में equally खिंचता है, तो उस पर net force zero।
पर surface पर एक molecule के नीचे और बगल में liquid है, और ऊपर सिर्फ air।
<excited> ऊपर खींचने वाले neighbours न होने से, उसे net inward pull महसूस होता है। हर surface molecule bulk की ओर खिंचता है।
तो surface कसकर तन जाती है, ढोल की खाल की तरह, और liquids अपना surface area कम से कम करते हैं।
एक free drop, बिना किसी और constraint के, ख़ुद को sphere में खींच लेती है, क्योंकि given volume के लिए sphere का surface area सबसे कम होता है।

board_events.text: Equally, each unit of new area stores a fixed energy.
The two views are numerically identical.
Surface tension equals surface energy per unit area.
Both measurements give the same value.

segments.text: <curious> Picture the surface as a perpetually shrinking sheet of stretched rubber.
Cut an imaginary line anywhere on it, and the rubber on each side pulls the other inward, perpendicular to the line.
The force per unit length of that line is the surface tension, S.
In symbols, S equals F over L, in newtons per metre.
That is one face of the coin. The second: every unit of new surface area you create stores a fixed amount of potential energy, the surface energy.
The two views are numerically identical.
<excited> Surface tension, force per length, equals surface energy, energy per area. The same number, whichever way you measure it.
Pull a wire to stretch a film and count the work; you get the same value as measuring force per length directly.
<curious> Surface को हमेशा सिकुड़ती हुई stretched rubber की एक sheet समझो।
उस पर कहीं भी एक imaginary line काटो, और दोनों तरफ की rubber एक दूसरे को inward खींचती है, line के perpendicular।
उस line की per unit length force ही surface tension है, S।
Symbols में, S equals F over L, newtons per metre में।
ये coin का एक चेहरा है। दूसरा: जो भी new surface area तुम बनाते हो, उसकी हर unit एक तय potential energy store करती है, surface energy।
दोनों views numerically identical हैं।
<excited> Surface tension, force per length, equals surface energy, energy per area। वही number, चाहे जिस तरह measure करो।
एक wire खींचकर film stretch करो और work गिनो; वही value मिलती है जो force per length सीधे measure करने से।

sections.title: Excess pressure in drops and bubbles

board_events.text: Excess pressure in drops and bubbles
A curved surface has higher pressure on its concave side.

board_events.caption: Drop is 2S/r, bubble is 4S/r

board_events.text: A soap bubble has two surfaces, so twice the excess.
An air bubble inside a liquid has one surface, like a drop.
Always ask: how many surfaces?

segments.text: <curious> This one idea blossoms into three big consequences. Here is the first.
A curved liquid surface has higher pressure on its concave side. The membrane's inward squeeze must be balanced by extra internal pressure.
That extra push is the excess pressure inside drops and bubbles.
For a liquid drop, with a single surface, the excess pressure is two S over r.
For a soap bubble, it is four S over r.
<excited> The difference is purely the surface count: a soap bubble has an inner and an outer surface, so twice the excess of a drop.
An air bubble inside a liquid has only one surface, so its excess is two S over r, just like a drop.
Always ask: how many surfaces? That alone decides the factor of two.
<curious> ये एक idea तीन बड़े consequences में खिलती है। ये रहा पहला।
एक curved liquid surface के concave side पर pressure ज़्यादा होता है। Membrane का inward squeeze extra internal pressure से balance होना चाहिए।
वही extra push drops और bubbles के अंदर का excess pressure है।
एक liquid drop के लिए, single surface के साथ, excess pressure two S over r है।
एक soap bubble के लिए, ये four S over r है।
<excited> फ़र्क़ सिर्फ surface count का है: soap bubble के inner और outer, दो surfaces होते हैं, तो drop से दोगुना excess।
Liquid के अंदर एक air bubble का सिर्फ एक surface होता है, तो इसका excess two S over r है, बिल्कुल drop जैसा।
हमेशा पूछो: कितने surfaces? वही अकेला factor of two तय करता है।

sections.title: Angle of contact: cohesion versus adhesion

board_events.text: Angle of contact
Cohesion pulls the liquid inward; adhesion clings to the solid.

board_events.caption: Water concave, mercury convex

board_events.text: Adhesion wins (water on glass): concave meniscus.
Wetting: angle of contact under 90 degrees.
Cohesion wins (mercury on glass): convex meniscus.
Non-wetting: angle of contact over 90 degrees.
Acute wets, obtuse will not; the angle falls with temperature.

segments.text: <curious> The second consequence. When a liquid meets a solid, two forces compete.
Cohesion is the liquid pulling on itself; adhesion is the liquid clinging to the solid. Their balance sets the angle of contact.
Compare water and mercury on glass.
If adhesion wins, as for water on clean glass, the liquid climbs the wall and the surface curves upward, concave.
That is wetting, with an acute angle of contact, under ninety degrees.
If cohesion wins, as for mercury on glass, the liquid pulls away and the surface bulges down, convex.
<excited> That is non-wetting, an obtuse angle over ninety degrees. Mercury on glass is about one hundred thirty five degrees.
So acute wets, obtuse will not. And the angle of contact decreases as temperature rises, part of why hot water cleans better.
<curious> दूसरा consequence। जब liquid किसी solid से मिलता है, दो forces मुक़ाबला करती हैं।
Cohesion यानी liquid का ख़ुद पर खिंचाव; adhesion यानी liquid का solid से चिपकना। इनका balance angle of contact तय करता है।
Glass पर water और mercury की तुलना करो।
अगर adhesion जीते, जैसे clean glass पर water, तो liquid दीवार चढ़ता है और surface ऊपर मुड़ती है, concave।
यही wetting है, acute angle of contact के साथ, ninety degrees से कम।
अगर cohesion जीते, जैसे glass पर mercury, तो liquid दूर हटता है और surface नीचे उभरती है, convex।
<excited> यही non-wetting है, obtuse angle ninety degrees से ऊपर। Glass पर mercury लगभग one hundred thirty five degrees।
तो acute wets, obtuse नहीं। और angle of contact temperature बढ़ने पर घटता है, यही एक वजह है कि गरम पानी बेहतर साफ़ करता है।

board_events.text: Capillarity
In a narrow tube, wall-climbing plus tension drags the column up.

board_events.caption: Water rises, mercury is depressed

board_events.text: A fine tube lifts water above, or depresses mercury below.
This carries water up soil to plant roots, oil up a wick.
The narrower the tube, the higher the rise.
Three consequences from one idea.

segments.text: <curious> The third consequence, and a lovely one, capillarity.
In a narrow tube, the wall-climbing of a wetting liquid, plus the surface tension, drags the whole liquid column upward.
For a wetting liquid like water, the column rises. For mercury, which does not wet glass, it is pushed down instead.
So a fine tube can lift water above the outside level, or depress mercury below it.
<excited> This is the mechanism that carries water up the soil to plant roots, and oil up a lamp wick.
And the narrower the tube, the higher the rise, an inverse relationship we will make precise with Jurin's law.
Three consequences from one idea: excess pressure, the angle of contact, and now capillarity.
<curious> तीसरा consequence, और एक प्यारा, capillarity।
एक narrow tube में, wetting liquid का दीवार चढ़ना, plus surface tension, पूरे liquid column को ऊपर खींचता है।
Water जैसे wetting liquid के लिए, column ऊपर उठता है। Mercury के लिए, जो glass को wet नहीं करता, ये नीचे धकेला जाता है।
तो एक fine tube water को बाहर के level से ऊपर उठा सकती है, या mercury को उससे नीचे दबा सकती है।
<excited> यही वो mechanism है जो पानी को soil के ज़रिए plant roots तक, और तेल को lamp wick पर चढ़ाता है।
और tube जितनी narrow, rise उतना ऊँचा, एक inverse relationship जिसे हम Jurin's law से precise करेंगे।
एक idea से तीन consequences: excess pressure, angle of contact, और अब capillarity।

A soap film on a U-frame with a sliding wire of length l; two faces.

board_events.text: Pull the wire out by x against the film's inward pull.

board_events.latex: W = F x = 2 S l x
2 S l x = E\,(2 l x)

board_events.text: So S = E: surface tension equals surface energy per area.

segments.text: <curious> Let us prove that surface tension equals surface energy per unit area.
Stretch a soap film on a U-frame with a sliding wire of length l. It has two faces, front and back.
The film pulls the wire inward, and you pull outward to stretch it.
Pull the wire out by a small distance x against that inward pull.
The film's inward force is two S times l, the factor two for the two surfaces.
The work done is force times distance, two S l times x.
This equals the surface energy times the new area, which over both faces is two l x. So two S l x equals E times two l x.
<excited> The two l x cancels, leaving S equals E. Surface tension equals surface energy per unit area, numerically and dimensionally.
<curious> चलो साबित करते हैं कि surface tension surface energy per unit area के बराबर है।
एक U-frame पर length l की sliding wire के साथ soap film stretch करो। इसके दो faces हैं, front और back।
Film wire को inward खींचती है, और तुम उसे stretch करने के लिए outward खींचते हो।
उस inward pull के ख़िलाफ़ wire को small distance x बाहर खींचो।
Film की inward force two S times l है, factor two दो surfaces के लिए।
किया गया work force times distance है, two S l times x।
ये surface energy times new area के बराबर है, जो दोनों faces पर two l x है। तो two S l x equals E times two l x।
<excited> two l x cancel हो जाता है, बचता है S equals E। Surface tension surface energy per unit area के बराबर है, numerically और dimensionally।

segments.text: <curious> Now derive the four S over r for a soap bubble.
Take a spherical soap bubble of radius R in equilibrium, and cut it into two hemispheres. A soap bubble has two liquid-air surfaces.
Consider one hemisphere. Two forces act across the flat circular boundary where it joins the other half.
The surface tension pulls the halves together, around the circumference two pi R, for each of the two surfaces.
So the surface-tension force is two times two pi R S, which is four pi R S.
The excess pressure pushes them apart, acting over the projected circular area pi R squared.
In equilibrium the two balance: delta P times pi R squared equals four pi R S.
<excited> Solving, the excess pressure is four S over R. For a drop, with one surface, the pull is halved to two S over R. The factor of two is purely the surface count.
<curious> अब soap bubble के लिए four S over r derive करते हैं।
Equilibrium में radius R की एक spherical soap bubble लो, और इसे दो hemispheres में काटो। एक soap bubble के दो liquid-air surfaces होते हैं।
एक hemisphere लो। उस flat circular boundary के across दो forces act करती हैं जहाँ वो दूसरे half से जुड़ता है।
Surface tension halves को साथ खींचती है, circumference two pi R के आसपास, दोनों surfaces में से हर एक के लिए।
तो surface-tension force two times two pi R S है, जो four pi R S है।
Excess pressure उन्हें अलग धकेलता है, projected circular area pi R squared पर act करते हुए।
Equilibrium में दोनों balance: delta P times pi R squared equals four pi R S।
<excited> Solve करने पर, excess pressure four S over R है। एक drop के लिए, एक surface के साथ, pull आधा होकर two S over R। Factor of two सिर्फ surface count है।

segments.text: <curious> Finally, derive the capillary rise, Jurin's law.
Dip a clean narrow tube of radius r into a wetting liquid, angle of contact theta. The meniscus is a spherical cap of radius R equals r over cos theta.
Just below the concave meniscus, the pressure is lower than atmospheric by the excess pressure, two S over R.
Outside the tube, just below the flat surface, the pressure is atmospheric.
Since pressure must be equal at the same level in the connected liquid, liquid climbs the tube to make up the deficit.
It rises until the weight of the raised column gives a matching hydrostatic pressure: rho g h equals two S over R, which is two S cos theta over r.
Solving, h equals two S cos theta, over r rho g. This is Jurin's law.
<excited> Since h goes as one over r, the narrower the tube, the higher the rise. For mercury, with theta over ninety degrees, cos theta is negative and h is negative, a depression.
<curious> आख़िर में, capillary rise, Jurin's law derive करते हैं।
Radius r की एक clean narrow tube को एक wetting liquid में डुबोओ, angle of contact theta। Meniscus radius R equals r over cos theta का एक spherical cap है।
Concave meniscus के ठीक नीचे, pressure atmospheric से excess pressure, two S over R, कम है।
Tube के बाहर, flat surface के ठीक नीचे, pressure atmospheric है।
चूँकि connected liquid में same level पर pressure equal होना चाहिए, liquid tube चढ़कर उस deficit की भरपाई करता है।
ये तब तक उठता है जब raised column का weight एक matching hydrostatic pressure दे: rho g h equals two S over R, यानी two S cos theta over r।
Solve करने पर, h equals two S cos theta, over r rho g। यही Jurin's law है।
<excited> चूँकि h one over r के साथ जाता है, tube जितनी narrow, rise उतना ऊँचा। Mercury के लिए, theta ninety degrees से ऊपर, cos theta negative और h negative, एक depression।

board_events.text: The surface tension toolkit
Angle of contact: acute wets, obtuse does not.
Surface tension falls with temperature, zero at critical.

segments.text: <curious> Let us gather the surface tension toolkit.
Surface tension is force per length, S equals F over L, with dimensions M T to the minus two.
Surface energy equals surface tension numerically, energy per unit area.
Excess pressure: two S over r for a drop or an air bubble, four S over r for a soap bubble with its two surfaces.
To detach a wire of length l takes two S l; a thin ring takes four pi r S, for its inner and outer edges.
Angle of contact: acute means wetting, a concave meniscus, a rise; obtuse means non-wetting, a convex meniscus, a depression.
Capillary rise, Jurin's law: h equals two S cos theta, over r rho g, with h inversely proportional to the radius.
<whisper> And two behaviours to remember: surface tension falls with temperature, reaching zero at the critical temperature, and soluble impurities raise it while soap lowers it.
<curious> Surface tension toolkit इकट्ठा कर लेते हैं।
Surface tension force per length है, S equals F over L, dimensions M T to the minus two।
Surface energy numerically surface tension के बराबर है, energy per unit area।
Excess pressure: drop या air bubble के लिए two S over r, दो surfaces वाली soap bubble के लिए four S over r।
Length l की wire को detach करने में two S l लगता है; एक thin ring में four pi r S, इसके inner और outer edges के लिए।
Angle of contact: acute यानी wetting, concave meniscus, rise; obtuse यानी non-wetting, convex meniscus, depression।
Capillary rise, Jurin's law: h equals two S cos theta, over r rho g, h radius के inversely proportional।
<whisper> और याद रखने लायक दो behaviours: surface tension temperature के साथ गिरती है, critical temperature पर zero तक, और soluble impurities इसे बढ़ाती हैं जबकि soap घटाता है।

Water would rise eight centimetres in a given tube. The tube is cut so only five centimetres projects above the surface. Does the water overflow?
The key idea: water never overflows from a short tube.
The product of the rise and the meniscus radius is fixed by the surface tension, h R equals two S over rho g, a constant.
If the available length is less than the natural rise, the water climbs to the top and the meniscus flattens, its radius increasing, until equilibrium is restored.
With natural rise eight and tube length five, the new meniscus radius is the tube radius times eight over five, that is one point six r.

Key idea: छोटी tube से पानी कभी overflow नहीं करता।
Rise और meniscus radius का product surface tension से तय है, h R equals two S over rho g, एक constant।
अगर available length natural rise से कम है, तो पानी top तक चढ़ता है और meniscus flatten होता है, इसका radius बढ़ता है, जब तक equilibrium बहाल न हो।
Natural rise eight और tube length five के साथ, नया meniscus radius tube radius times eight over five है, यानी one point six r।
<excited> तो पानी top तक, five centimetres, चढ़कर रुक जाता है। Meniscus कम curved हो जाता है। No overflow, इस trap का classic हल।

segments.text: <curious> A two-part J E E Advanced problem: rise between plates, then a double bubble.
Part a: two parallel glass plates a small distance d apart are dipped in water, angle of contact zero. Find the rise between them.
Between plates the meniscus is cylindrical, curved in one direction only, so the excess pressure below it is S over R with R equal to d over two.
Balancing against the raised column gives two S over d equals rho g h, so h is two S over rho g d. Note the contrast with a tube, which has two curvatures.
Part b: two soap bubbles of radii a and b, with a bigger, coalesce and share a common film. Find its radius of curvature.
The smaller bubble has the larger internal excess pressure, since four S over r grows as r shrinks. So air pushes from the small bubble toward the large one.
The excess pressure across the common film equals the difference: four S over R equals four S over b minus four S over a, so R is a b over a minus b.
<excited> The common film curves toward, and bulges into, the bigger bubble, with radius a b over a minus b, a standard Advanced result.
<curious> दो हिस्सों वाला J E E Advanced problem: plates के बीच rise, फिर एक double bubble।
Part a: distance d की दूरी पर दो parallel glass plates water में डूबी हैं, angle of contact zero। इनके बीच rise निकालो।
Plates के बीच meniscus cylindrical है, सिर्फ एक direction में curved, तो इसके नीचे excess pressure S over R है, R equal to d over two।
Raised column के ख़िलाफ़ balance करने से two S over d equals rho g h, तो h two S over rho g d है। Tube से contrast देखो, जिसके दो curvatures हैं।
Part b: radii a और b की दो soap bubbles, a बड़ी, मिलकर एक common film share करती हैं। इसका radius of curvature निकालो।
छोटी bubble का internal excess pressure बड़ा होता है, क्योंकि four S over r, r घटते ही बढ़ता है। तो air छोटी bubble से बड़ी की ओर धकेलती है।
Common film के across excess pressure difference के बराबर है: four S over R equals four S over b minus four S over a, तो R a b over a minus b है।
<excited> Common film बड़ी bubble की ओर मुड़कर उसमें उभरता है, radius a b over a minus b के साथ, एक standard Advanced result।

board_events.text: Pitfalls and pro-tips
A soap bubble has two surfaces: excess 4S/r, not 2S/r.
Jurin: rise goes as 1/r; narrower tubes rise higher.
Acute angle wets and rises; obtuse does not and is depressed.
Tube radius is not the meniscus radius unless angle is zero.
Before any calculation: how many surfaces, and is the angle zero?
For ratios, both excess pressure and rise go as 1/r.

segments.text: <curious> Let us lock in the surface tension traps, and the first is everywhere.

First, the soap bubble's two surfaces. Its excess pressure is four S over r, and the work to blow it uses twice the sphere area. A drop or an air bubble has one surface, two S over r. Always ask how many surfaces.
Second, inverting Jurin's law. Capillary rise goes as one over r, so narrower tubes rise higher, not lower. The intuitive guess, bigger tube more water, is exactly wrong.
Third, the angle of contact. Acute, under ninety degrees, means wetting, concave, a rise. Obtuse, over ninety, means non-wetting, convex, a depression.

Fourth, tube radius versus meniscus radius. In the capillary formula r is the tube radius, but the excess pressure uses the meniscus radius, R equals r over cos theta. They are equal only when the angle is zero.
So run a two-second checklist before any calculation: how many surfaces, and is the angle of contact zero?
<whisper> And for ratio questions, lean on the scalings: excess pressure goes as one over r, and capillary rise goes as one over r. You can often answer without ever computing S.
<curious> Surface tension के traps पक्के कर लेते हैं, और पहला हर जगह है।

पहला, soap bubble के दो surfaces। इसका excess pressure four S over r है, और फुलाने का work sphere area का दोगुना use करता है। Drop या air bubble का एक surface, two S over r। हमेशा पूछो कितने surfaces।
दूसरा, Jurin's law को उल्टा करना। Capillary rise one over r के साथ जाता है, तो narrower tubes ऊँचा उठते हैं, नीचे नहीं। Intuitive अंदाज़ा, बड़ी tube ज़्यादा पानी, बिल्कुल गलत है।
तीसरा, angle of contact। Acute, ninety degrees से कम, यानी wetting, concave, एक rise। Obtuse, ninety से ऊपर, यानी non-wetting, convex, एक depression।
चौथा, tube radius बनाम meniscus radius। Capillary formula में r tube radius है, पर excess pressure meniscus radius use करता है, R equals r over cos theta। ये सिर्फ तब equal हैं जब angle zero हो।
तो किसी भी calculation से पहले दो-second checklist चलाओ: कितने surfaces, और क्या angle of contact zero है?
<whisper> और ratio questions के लिए scalings पर टिको: excess pressure one over r, और capillary rise one over r के साथ जाता है। अक्सर S निकाले बिना ही answer दे सकते हो।

board_events.text: Chapter cheat sheet
Pressure is a scalar; deeper is denser-times-g-times-depth.
Buoyancy belongs to the fluid; sink if denser, float if lighter.
Liquid lags and rises at the rear; free fall, no pressure.
Fast and low, slow and high; continuity first, Bernoulli second.
Terminal velocity goes as r squared; liquids loosen, gases gum up.
Flow goes as radius to the fourth; add resistances in series.
Bubble is 4, drop is 2; narrow tube, high climb.

segments.text: <curious> And a one-breath cheat sheet, the memory aids that carry the whole chapter.
Pressure is a scalar, and deeper means denser times g times depth. One atmosphere per ten metres in water.
Buoyancy belongs to the fluid, not the body. Sink if denser, float if lighter, and the submerged fraction is the density ratio.
In an accelerating tank the liquid lags and rises at the rear. In free fall, no pressure. Spin makes a parabola.
For flow: fast and low, slow and high. Solve continuity first, then Bernoulli. Efflux is free fall.
Terminal velocity goes as r squared. Liquids loosen when heated, gases gum up.
Poiseuille flow goes as radius to the fourth. Add resistances in series, reciprocal-add in parallel.
<excited> And for surface tension: bubble is four, drop is two, for excess pressure. Narrow tube, high climb. Acute wets, obtuse will not. That is the whole chapter in a handful of lines.
